objectives.title: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

videos.title: An Overview of Malware
videos.summary: Messer introduces malware as a category, explains how it gets onto a system, and walks through the main families the exam expects you to recognise: ransomware, trojans, worms, spyware, bloatware, viruses, keyloggers, logic bombs and rootkits.
videos.deepDive:
Malware is simply software that does something the owner of the machine did not consent to. The exam cares less about the definition and more about whether you can look at a scenario and name the family. The trick is to classify by how it spreads and what it does once it is running, because those two axes separate almost every type.

Spread mechanisms fall into three groups. A virus attaches itself to a file or program and needs a human to run that file. A worm spreads on its own across a network by exploiting a vulnerability, with no user action at all. A trojan does not spread by itself; it tricks a person into installing it by pretending to be something useful, such as a cracked copy of Microsoft Office or a fake bank statement PDF. Once you fix the spread mechanism in your head, the payload is a separate question. The same trojan might drop a keylogger, a ransomware encryptor or a remote-access tool.

Payload behaviours are what the rest of this objective drills into. Ransomware encrypts data and demands payment. Spyware and keyloggers quietly collect information. A logic bomb waits for a trigger such as a date or an employee record being deleted from HR. A rootkit hides itself and other malware by modifying the operating system or kernel. Bloatware is not strictly malicious but is unwanted software that ships pre-installed and expands the attack surface.

Worked example: a finance officer at a Lagos microfinance bank receives an email that appears to come from a vendor, with an attachment named Invoice_Sept.pdf.exe. She double-clicks it. Nothing visible happens, but the file drops a second executable into C:\Users\Public, adds a Run key in the registry for persistence and begins beaconing to an external IP on port 443 every 60 seconds. Classification: the delivery was a trojan (it pretended to be an invoice). The beaconing behaviour suggests a remote-access payload. If it then starts scanning the LAN on port 445 and copying itself to other hosts, a worm component has been added.

What this looks like to a SOC analyst: the EDR alert fires on a process launched from a user-writable directory, the parent process is Outlook or a browser, and there is a new autorun entry. In the SIEM you would pivot on the host, the user and the destination IP, check whether any other host contacted the same IP, and look at proxy logs for the initial download. Triage moves from confirm it is real (hash lookup, sandbox detonation) to scope it (who else) to contain it (isolate the host through EDR, block the IP and domain at the firewall and proxy).

Mitigation is layered because no single control catches every family: user awareness reduces trojan success, patching kills worms, application allow lists stop unknown executables from launching, EDR watches behaviour rather than signatures, and tested offline backups make ransomware survivable. On the exam, when a scenario says the malware arrived disguised as legitimate software, answer trojan; when it moved across the network with no clicks, answer worm; when it needed a file to be opened, answer virus.

keyTerms.def: Any software intentionally designed to damage, disrupt, spy on or gain unauthorised access to a system.
Malware disguised as legitimate software that relies on the user to install it and does not self-replicate.
Self-replicating malware that spreads across networks by exploiting vulnerabilities without any user action.
Malware that attaches to a file or program and replicates only when a user executes the infected host file.
The part of malware that performs the actual malicious action once the malware is running.
A technique such as a registry Run key or scheduled task that lets malware survive a reboot.
The channel malware uses to receive instructions from and send data to an attacker-controlled server.
A small initial program whose only job is to install other malware on the system.

examTips: Classify by spread first: needs a user to run a file = virus, spreads alone over the network = worm, pretends to be useful software = trojan.
A scenario describing regular outbound connections at fixed intervals to an unknown external IP is pointing at command-and-control beaconing.
Do not confuse bloatware with malware; bloatware is unwanted and risky but not designed to be malicious.
The exam frequently combines families, for example a trojan that installs a rootkit; answer based on the specific behaviour the question asks about.
videos.realWorld: In a bank SOC, most malware cases start as an EDR or email-gateway alert rather than a user report. The analyst confirms the file hash against threat intelligence, checks whether the process tree makes sense (a spreadsheet spawning PowerShell does not), then scopes across the estate before isolating the host. GRC teams care about the same case from a different angle: was the control that failed documented, is there a CBN or NDPA notification duty if customer data was touched, and does the incident register capture the root cause for the next audit?

quiz.q: A user downloads what appears to be a free PDF converter from a forum. After installation the SOC observes the host making outbound HTTPS connections to an unknown IP every 30 seconds. No other hosts are affected. Which type of malware best describes the initial infection?
quiz.explain: The user was tricked into installing software that looked useful, which is the definition of a trojan. A worm would spread to other hosts on its own, a virus needs an infected host file, and a logic bomb waits for a trigger condition rather than beaconing immediately.

quiz.q: Overnight, 40 servers in a data centre become infected with no user interaction. Investigation shows the malware exploited an unpatched SMB vulnerability to copy itself between hosts. What is this?
quiz.explain: Self-replication across the network with no user action by exploiting a vulnerability is the defining behaviour of a worm. Trojans require a user to install them, rootkits hide malware rather than spread it, and spyware collects data.

quiz.q: An analyst finds a new registry Run key pointing to an executable in a user's temp folder. What is the primary purpose of this artefact from the attacker's perspective?
quiz.explain: A Run key causes the executable to launch each time the user logs in, which keeps the malware alive after a reboot. That is persistence. It does not by itself raise privileges, move data out or reach other hosts.

videos.title: Viruses and Worms
videos.summary: Messer contrasts viruses, which need a user to run an infected file, with worms, which self-propagate across networks, and describes sub-types such as boot sector, script, macro and fileless viruses.
videos.deepDive:
The single most tested distinction in this section is that a virus requires human action and a worm does not. Everything else is detail layered on top of that.

A virus is code that inserts itself into another file or program. When the user opens that file, the virus runs, then usually copies itself into other files so it survives and spreads. Sub-types are named after where they live. A program virus infects executables. A boot sector virus writes itself into the master boot record so it loads before the operating system. A script virus is written in JavaScript, VBScript or PowerShell and runs inside a browser or the Windows Script Host. A macro virus lives inside an Office document and runs when macros are enabled; this is why Microsoft now blocks macros from internet-sourced files by default. A fileless virus never writes a file to disk at all; it runs in memory, typically through PowerShell or WMI, and persists through the registry or scheduled tasks. Fileless malware matters because traditional antivirus scans files on disk and has nothing to scan.

A worm carries its own propagation engine. It scans for reachable hosts, checks whether each one is vulnerable to a specific exploit, delivers the exploit, and repeats from the new host. Because there is no human in the loop, worms move at machine speed. WannaCry in 2017 used the EternalBlue SMB exploit to compromise around 200,000 systems in a day; many of those systems had a patch available for two months. The worm carried a ransomware payload, which is why you will see it described as both.

Worked example of a macro virus in a bank: a credit analyst receives Loan_Book_Q3.xlsm from what looks like a colleague. She enables content. The macro uses Shell to run an encoded PowerShell command that downloads a second-stage payload. In the SIEM this appears as EXCEL.EXE spawning powershell.exe with a -EncodedCommand argument (Sysmon Event ID 1 or Windows Security 4688 with command-line auditing on). That parent-child relationship is the signature; Excel has no legitimate reason to launch PowerShell.

Worm indicators are different. You would see one host suddenly generating thousands of connection attempts to port 445 or 3389 across the subnet (firewall or NetFlow logs), IDS signatures for the exploit firing repeatedly, and then the same behaviour appearing on the hosts it reached. The spread pattern itself is the indicator, and speed of containment matters more than perfect analysis. A SOC analyst would block the port at the internal segmentation firewall, isolate the source host, and then work backwards.

Mitigation for viruses is mostly about the human and the endpoint: security awareness, blocking macros and script hosts by policy, and EDR that watches process behaviour rather than just file hashes. Mitigation for worms is mostly about the network: patch the exploited vulnerability, segment the network so one subnet cannot reach every other, and disable unneeded services so there is nothing to exploit. On the exam, if the scenario mentions patching as the fix, it is nearly always a worm.

keyTerms.def: A virus that infects the master boot record so it executes before the operating system loads.
A virus written in the macro language of an application such as Microsoft Office and triggered when the document's macros run.
A virus written in a scripting language such as PowerShell, VBScript or JavaScript.
Malware that runs entirely in memory using built-in tools like PowerShell, leaving no executable on disk for antivirus to scan.
The ability of a worm to locate and infect new hosts without any human involvement.
The SMBv1 exploit used by the WannaCry worm in 2017 to spread across unpatched Windows systems.
Using tools already present on the system, such as PowerShell or WMI, to avoid dropping detectable files.

examTips: User double-clicked, opened, enabled content or ran something = virus. Spread with zero user action = worm.
Fileless malware is tested as the reason signature-based antivirus fails; the answer is behaviour-based EDR.
Macro virus scenarios usually mention Office documents and enabling content or macros.
If the remediation in the answer choices is patching or network segmentation, the question is describing a worm.
videos.realWorld: SOC analysts in fintechs spend a lot of time on Office-spawns-PowerShell alerts, because macro-based delivery is still one of the cheapest ways for criminals to get a foothold. A good detection rule looks at the parent process, the command-line flags and whether the script contacts the internet. Worm-style spread is rarer but far more dangerous, so segmentation between the card-processing network and the office LAN is something GRC teams verify during PCI DSS assessments and CBN risk-based supervision reviews.

quiz.q: A SIEM alert shows winword.exe launching powershell.exe with an encoded command shortly after a user opened an email attachment. There is no new file on disk. Which two descriptions fit this activity?
quiz.explain: A Word document launching PowerShell points to a macro virus, and the absence of any file on disk with execution in memory is the definition of fileless malware. Nothing in the scenario indicates self-propagation, a hidden kernel component or a trigger condition.

quiz.q: Within one hour, hundreds of workstations across multiple offices are compromised. Logs show each infected host scanning the subnet on TCP 445 before the next hosts become infected. Which action would have most directly prevented this?
options: Applying the vendor patch for the exploited SMB vulnerability
quiz.explain: The behaviour is a worm exploiting an SMB vulnerability. Patching removes the vulnerability the worm relies on. Disk encryption and password managers do not stop remote exploitation, and macros are irrelevant because no user action was involved.

quiz.q: Why does traditional signature-based antivirus often miss fileless malware?
options: Fileless malware runs only on Linux
There is no executable written to disk for the scanner to inspect
Fileless malware disables the antivirus service first
quiz.explain: Signature-based antivirus scans files on disk. Fileless malware executes in memory through legitimate tools such as PowerShell, so there is nothing on disk to match a signature against. The other options are not general properties of fileless malware.

videos.title: Spyware and Bloatware
videos.summary: Messer explains spyware as software that secretly monitors the user and sends data to a third party, and bloatware as unwanted pre-installed software that wastes resources and widens the attack surface.
videos.deepDive:
Spyware and bloatware sit at opposite ends of a spectrum. Spyware is designed to harm you by watching you. Bloatware is not designed to harm you, but it makes your system easier to harm. The exam tests whether you can tell them apart and whether you know why bloatware still matters.

Spyware collects information without consent and sends it somewhere. Common forms include browser monitoring that records every site visited, keyloggers that capture keystrokes (covered in the next video), and identity-theft tools that scrape saved passwords, browser cookies and autofill data. Spyware usually arrives bundled with something the user wanted: a free screen recorder, a cracked game, a browser toolbar that promises coupons. Some spyware is commercial, marketed as parental monitoring or employee monitoring, and becomes malicious only because it is installed without the target's knowledge; this category is sometimes called stalkerware.

How spyware behaves once running: it hooks into the browser or the operating system to observe activity, stores what it captures in a local file or in memory, and periodically uploads to a collection server. That upload is your best detection opportunity. Spyware on a bank teller's workstation might upload a few hundred kilobytes every hour to a domain registered three days ago. In proxy logs you would see repeated POST requests to an unfamiliar host, often at very regular intervals, from a process that is not a browser. Windows Event 4688 with command-line logging, or Sysmon Event 3 (network connection), lets you tie the connection to the process.

Bloatware is the trial antivirus, the vendor update utility, the games and the promotional apps that ship on a new laptop or phone. Three problems follow. First, it consumes CPU, memory and disk, which slows the machine and sometimes causes users to disable security tools they blame for the slowness. Second, every extra program is extra code that may contain vulnerabilities; the 2015 Superfish incident is the textbook case, where a pre-installed advertising tool on Lenovo laptops shipped with a self-signed root certificate and its private key, allowing anyone to intercept HTTPS traffic on those machines. Third, bloatware often runs with high privileges and auto-updates from vendor servers, which is exactly the kind of trusted channel supply-chain attackers like to hijack.

Worked SOC scenario: a compliance officer reports her laptop is slow. The analyst checks the process list and finds 14 startup items, including a vendor photo app, a trial VPN, and a browser extension called Deal Finder. The extension is uploading the URL of every page she visits, including internal SharePoint links, to an ad-tech domain. The photo app is a year out of date and has a known privilege-escalation flaw. Classification: the extension is spyware, the rest is bloatware. Remediation is removal, followed by a policy decision.

Mitigation for both is the same discipline. Build a standard image that contains only approved software and re-image new hardware rather than using the vendor build. Enforce an application allow list so unapproved software cannot run. Use browser policies to block unapproved extensions. For spyware specifically, EDR with behavioural detection and DNS filtering catches the upload phase. For bloatware, the fix is a hardening standard that removes unnecessary software, which links directly to objective 2.5.

keyTerms.def: Software that covertly monitors user activity and transmits the collected data to a third party without consent.
Unwanted software pre-installed by a manufacturer or vendor that consumes resources and increases the attack surface without being inherently malicious.
Software that displays or injects advertisements, often bundled with free applications and frequently overlapping with spyware behaviour.
Commercial monitoring software installed on a device without the owner's knowledge to track their activity.
The total set of points where an attacker could try to enter or extract data from a system; every extra program enlarges it.
A pre-approved operating system build containing only sanctioned software, used instead of the vendor default.
The 2015 Lenovo pre-installed adware that included a root certificate and private key, enabling interception of HTTPS traffic.

examTips: Spyware questions describe secret collection and sending of data; bloatware questions describe pre-installed, resource-hungry, unnecessary software.
The correct fix for bloatware in answer choices is usually removing unnecessary software or deploying a standard corporate image.
Bloatware is tested as an attack-surface problem, not as malware; do not pick antivirus as the remedy.
A browser toolbar or extension that tracks browsing is spyware even if the user technically agreed to a long licence.
videos.realWorld: Endpoint teams at Nigerian banks typically wipe every new laptop and apply a golden image precisely to strip vendor bloatware, and the GRC function documents that image as part of the hardening baseline auditors ask for. On the SOC side, spyware most often surfaces as a data-loss or proxy alert: a process nobody recognises posting to an advertising or unknown domain from a workstation that handles customer data, which under the NDPA can turn a nuisance into a reportable incident.

quiz.q: A new batch of laptops arrives with a trial security suite, a vendor game hub and several promotional apps pre-installed. The security team is concerned. What is the most appropriate description of the risk and the best response?
options: There is no risk because the software is from the manufacturer
The apps are spyware; run a malware scan
The apps are bloatware that expands the attack surface; re-image with the corporate standard build
The apps are trojans; block them at the firewall
quiz.explain: Pre-installed unnecessary software is bloatware. It is not malicious by design but adds vulnerable code and consumes resources. The standard remediation is to remove it, ideally by deploying a clean corporate image. Manufacturer origin does not mean the software is safe, as the Superfish case showed.

quiz.q: A user installed a free video downloader. Since then, proxy logs show the host sending small POST requests every ten minutes to a recently registered domain, and the data includes the titles of documents the user opened. What has been installed?
quiz.explain: Secret collection of user activity and transmission to a third party is spyware. Bloatware does not exfiltrate activity data, ransomware encrypts files and demands payment, and a logic bomb waits for a trigger.

quiz.q: Which control most directly prevents users from installing browser extensions that track their browsing?
options: A managed browser policy that allows only approved extensions
quiz.explain: A centrally managed browser policy with an extension allow list stops unapproved extensions from being installed at all. Disk encryption, segmentation and password policy do not control what runs in the browser.

videos.title: Other Malware Types
videos.summary: Messer covers the remaining families on the objective list: keyloggers, logic bombs, rootkits and ransomware, describing how each one operates and how to detect and defend against it.
videos.deepDive:
This video sweeps up four families that behave very differently, so treat them as four separate mental models rather than one topic.

Keyloggers record keystrokes and increasingly also clipboard contents, screenshots and form data. Software keyloggers hook the keyboard driver or use accessibility APIs; hardware keyloggers are small devices inserted between the keyboard and the USB port that no software scanner can see. The classic value for an attacker is credentials, because a keylogger captures the password before it is ever hashed or encrypted. Detection is behavioural: a process reading keyboard input that is not in the foreground, a local file growing steadily, and periodic uploads. Mitigation includes EDR, MFA (a stolen password alone becomes useless), and physical inspection of shared workstations such as branch teller terminals.

Logic bombs are dormant code that activates when a condition is met: a date, a time, a user account being disabled, a specific file being deleted. They are usually planted by insiders, often a system administrator who expects to be dismissed. The 2013 attack on South Korean banks wiped master boot records at a preset time. Logic bombs are hard to detect because until the trigger fires there is no malicious behaviour to observe. Defences are therefore procedural: code review and change control for scripts and scheduled tasks, separation of duties so no single admin can deploy unreviewed code to production, file integrity monitoring on critical systems, and prompt removal of access when someone leaves.

Rootkits modify the operating system, often at kernel level, to hide processes, files, registry keys and network connections from the tools an analyst would use. Because the rootkit sits below the tools, Task Manager, netstat and even some EDR agents report a clean system. Modern defences shifted the fight to boot time: UEFI Secure Boot verifies bootloader signatures, Windows driver signature enforcement blocks unsigned kernel modules, and measured boot reports hashes to a TPM. Detection often requires booting from clean media or comparing what the live OS reports to what a raw disk or memory image shows. Remediation is almost always a rebuild from a known-good image, not a cleanup.

Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment, and modern crews add double extortion: they steal data first and threaten to publish it. The chain is initial access (phishing, exposed RDP, a vulnerable VPN appliance), privilege escalation, disabling backups and security tools, then mass encryption. The SOC indicators come in order: unusual admin logons, vssadmin delete shadows or similar commands to remove Volume Shadow Copies, a spike in file rename and write operations from one process, and files appearing with a new extension. Encryption is the last step, so every earlier step is a chance to stop it.

Worked example: a Nigerian insurer's SOC sees a domain admin account log in at 02:15 from a server it never uses, followed by a scheduled task creation across 60 hosts. That is the deployment phase. Isolating the account and the source server at that moment prevents the encryption that would have run at 03:00. Mitigation for ransomware is a stack: MFA on remote access, patched edge devices, EDR, least privilege for admin accounts, tested offline or immutable backups, and a rehearsed incident response plan. The exam likes to ask which control lets you recover without paying; the answer is offline backups.

keyTerms.def: Hardware or software that records keystrokes, typically to capture credentials before they are encrypted.
Dormant malicious code that executes when a specific condition such as a date or event occurs, frequently planted by an insider.
Malware that modifies the operating system, often at kernel level, to conceal itself and other malicious components from detection tools.
Malware that encrypts data and demands payment for the decryption key, often combined with data theft for extortion.
A ransomware tactic of stealing data before encryption and threatening to publish it if the ransom is not paid.
A UEFI feature that verifies the digital signature of the bootloader and kernel to block rootkits that load before the OS.
Windows point-in-time file snapshots that ransomware commonly deletes to prevent easy recovery.
A backup copy that is disconnected from the network so it cannot be encrypted or deleted by ransomware.

examTips: Anything triggered by a date, time or event, especially involving a disgruntled employee, is a logic bomb.
If a scenario says security tools report the system is clean but there is clear evidence of compromise, think rootkit and answer with boot from trusted media or rebuild.
Ransomware recovery questions: the correct control is tested offline or immutable backups, not paying the ransom.
MFA is the exam's favourite answer for reducing the impact of a keylogger capturing a password.
videos.realWorld: Ransomware is the incident bank boards actually ask about, and CBN's risk-based cybersecurity framework expects documented backup and recovery testing for exactly this reason. In the SOC, the highest-value detections are the pre-encryption steps: shadow copy deletion, mass scheduled task creation, and admin logons at odd hours. GRC analysts turn those into control requirements, verify backups are restored in drills rather than assumed to work, and manage insider risk through leaver processes so that a departing administrator cannot leave a logic bomb behind.

quiz.q: A systems administrator is told his contract will not be renewed. Two weeks after he leaves, a script runs on the payroll server and deletes all records on the last day of the month. Which type of malware is this?
quiz.explain: Code that lies dormant and triggers on a specific condition, here a date, and is associated with a disgruntled insider is a logic bomb. There is no hiding behaviour (rootkit), self-spread (worm) or keystroke capture (keylogger).

quiz.q: An analyst sees outbound connections from a server in firewall logs, but netstat and the process list on the server show nothing unusual and the antivirus reports the system is clean. What is the most likely explanation and the best next step?
options: A logic bomb is waiting to trigger; wait and monitor
The firewall is misconfigured; ignore the alert
A rootkit is hiding the activity; analyse the system from trusted boot media or a disk image
The server needs more RAM; schedule maintenance
quiz.explain: When external evidence contradicts what the operating system reports, a rootkit is hiding the activity from the tools running on that OS. Examining the system from outside the compromised OS, by booting clean media or imaging the disk, reveals what the rootkit hides.

quiz.q: During an incident, the SOC sees the command vssadmin delete shadows /all executed on several file servers, followed by a rapid increase in file writes. What should the analyst conclude?
options: A keylogger is uploading captured data
Routine backup maintenance is in progress
Ransomware deployment is underway and hosts should be isolated immediately
quiz.explain: Deleting Volume Shadow Copies removes the easy recovery path and is a hallmark pre-encryption step for ransomware; the surge in file writes is the encryption itself. Immediate isolation limits how many files are encrypted.

videos.title: Physical Attacks
videos.summary: Messer covers attacks that need physical presence or proximity: brute-force entry against doors and locks, cloning of RFID badges and cards, and environmental attacks on power, cooling and fire systems.
videos.deepDive:
Security+ treats physical attacks as a distinct indicator category because the evidence lives in badge systems, CCTV and facility logs rather than in a SIEM. A SOC analyst at a bank still needs to recognise them, because a physical breach usually precedes a logical one. The objective names three: brute force, RFID cloning and environmental.

Physical brute force means overpowering a barrier rather than outsmarting it: kicking in a door, cutting a padlock, crowbarring a server rack, driving a vehicle through a fence. It also covers forcing a badge reader or lock until it fails open. The indicators are alarms, broken hardware, and gaps in CCTV coverage. Defence is layered deterrence and delay: solid doors with reinforced frames, bollards, mantraps (access control vestibules) that trap an intruder between two doors, guards, and alarms that alert before the attacker reaches anything valuable. The design principle is that each layer should buy more time than the response team needs to arrive.

RFID cloning targets the proximity badges most offices use. Older 125 kHz badges broadcast a fixed identifier with no encryption. An attacker with a handheld reader can capture that identifier by standing within a metre of the victim, in a lift or at a coffee shop, then write it to a blank card in seconds. The clone is indistinguishable to the door reader. Higher-frequency 13.56 MHz cards using DESFire or similar can be far harder to clone because they use mutual authentication with keys, but many are deployed in a legacy compatibility mode that defeats the point. Indicators of a cloned badge are the same as those for a stolen one: a badge used at two distant doors within an impossible time window, use outside the owner's normal hours, or use while the owner is on leave. Physical access control systems can feed these events into the SIEM, and the impossible-travel logic you use for VPN logins applies just as well to doors. Mitigation includes upgrading to encrypted smart cards, pairing badge with PIN or biometric at sensitive doors, RFID-blocking sleeves, and treating badge logs as security logs.

Environmental attacks attack the conditions equipment needs to run. Cutting power or tampering with the UPS, disabling or manipulating HVAC so a server room overheats, triggering a fire suppression discharge, or flooding a floor all cause outages without touching a single system. These are availability attacks and they are often insider-enabled or opportunistic during construction work. Indicators come from building management systems: temperature and humidity sensors, power quality alarms, water sensors, and door sensors on utility rooms. Mitigation is redundancy plus monitoring: dual power feeds, generators with fuel contracts, N+1 cooling, sensors that alert the SOC, and restricting physical access to plant rooms as tightly as to the data hall.

Worked example: a Lagos payment processor notices its primary data centre room hit 38 degrees at 01:00 on a Sunday. The building management alert goes to facilities, not security. By the time anyone responds, two storage arrays have shut down on thermal protection. Investigation finds the HVAC controller was set to maintenance mode from a laptop connected in the plant room, which a contractor's badge had opened. Three lessons the exam expects you to draw: environmental alerts belong in the security monitoring pipeline, plant rooms need the same access control as server rooms, and contractor badges need expiry dates and scope limits.

keyTerms.def: Gaining entry by overpowering or breaking a physical barrier such as a door, lock or fence.
Capturing the identifier broadcast by a proximity badge and writing it to a blank card to impersonate the holder.
Disrupting power, cooling, fire suppression or other facility conditions to cause an outage.
A two-door entry where the second door opens only after the first closes, preventing tailgating and trapping intruders.
A short sturdy post that stops vehicles from ramming a building or barrier.
The control and monitoring system for HVAC, power and environmental sensors in a facility.
Following an authorised person through a controlled door without presenting credentials.

examTips: A badge used at two far-apart doors within minutes is the physical version of impossible travel and points to cloning or sharing.
Environmental attack questions are availability questions; look for answers involving redundancy and environmental monitoring.
Low-frequency 125 kHz badges are the cloneable ones; smart cards with mutual authentication are the fix.
A mantrap or access control vestibule is the exam's answer for preventing tailgating and forced entry.
videos.realWorld: Bank branch and data-centre security in Nigeria is usually handled by a separate physical security team, but mature SOCs ingest badge and BMS events so an analyst can correlate a server-room door opening with an unexpected console login two minutes later. GRC analysts audit badge lifecycle (issue, review, revoke), contractor access, and the environmental controls that PCI DSS, ISO 27001 Annex A and CBN data-centre guidance require, and they schedule generator and cooling failover tests the same way they schedule backup restores.

quiz.q: Badge logs show an employee's card opened the Abuja office door at 09:02 and the Lagos data centre door at 09:20 on the same day. The employee confirms she has been in Abuja all week. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The badge was cloned using an RFID reader
The employee tailgated into the data centre
An environmental attack triggered the door
The badge system clock is wrong
quiz.explain: The same credential used at two locations that cannot be reached in the elapsed time indicates the identifier was copied to a second card. Tailgating would not generate a badge event, and a clock error would not explain two cities. Environmental attacks target power and cooling, not doors.

quiz.q: A company wants to stop an attacker from simply forcing the front door and running into the office. Which control is most effective?
options: An access control vestibule with a guard
quiz.explain: A vestibule (mantrap) physically prevents passage until the person is verified and traps anyone who forces the outer door. Awareness training, disk encryption and PIN policy do not stop physical brute force.

quiz.q: Servers in a data hall shut down after the room temperature rose rapidly. Investigation finds the cooling system was switched off from the plant room. Which category of attack is this, and which control would most reduce the impact?
options: Denial of service; a web application firewall
Environmental attack; redundant cooling plus temperature alerts routed to the security team
RFID cloning; upgrade to smart cards
quiz.explain: Manipulating cooling to cause an outage is an environmental attack. N+1 cooling keeps the room within range if one unit fails or is disabled, and routing sensor alerts to the SOC ensures a fast response. The other options address different attack types.

videos.title: Denial of Service
videos.summary: Messer explains denial of service and distributed denial of service, how botnets generate volume, and how amplification and reflection let a small attacker produce very large floods.
videos.deepDive:
A denial of service (DoS) attack makes a service unavailable to its legitimate users. It does not need to steal anything. The attacker can exhaust bandwidth, exhaust server resources such as connections or CPU, or trigger a crash through a bug. When the traffic comes from many sources at once, it is a distributed denial of service (DDoS), usually generated by a botnet of compromised computers, routers and IoT devices whose owners have no idea they are participating.

DDoS attacks are classified by which layer they hit. Volumetric attacks fill the pipe with UDP floods or amplified traffic measured in gigabits per second. Protocol attacks exhaust state tables on servers or firewalls; a SYN flood sends thousands of connection openings and never completes the handshake, leaving half-open connections that consume memory. Application-layer attacks look like normal requests but are chosen to be expensive: repeated searches, login attempts, or slow HTTP requests (Slowloris) that hold connections open with partial headers. Application attacks need far less bandwidth and are harder to distinguish from real users.

The two words the exam requires are amplified and reflected. Reflection means the attacker sends requests with a spoofed source IP, the victim's address, to third-party servers. Those servers reply to the victim, so the victim sees traffic from hundreds of legitimate servers rather than from the attacker. Amplification means the reply is much bigger than the request. An open DNS resolver can turn a 60-byte query for an ANY record into a 3,000-byte response, a factor of about 50. Memcached servers exposed to the internet have produced amplification factors above 10,000 and were behind the 1.3 terabit per second attack on GitHub in 2018. NTP monlist, SSDP and CLDAP are other common reflectors. Put together: a botnet of 1,000 devices, each sending 1 Mbps of spoofed DNS queries, yields roughly 50 Gbps arriving at the victim from DNS servers all over the world.

Indicators in a SOC: a sudden jump in inbound traffic on network monitoring graphs, a flood of UDP packets from source port 53 or 123 that the victim never asked for, firewall state tables filling up, web server logs showing thousands of requests per second for one expensive URL, and users reporting timeouts. For an application-layer attack, look for many requests with identical user agents or request patterns and no normal browsing behaviour around them. Distinguishing a DDoS from a legitimate traffic spike, such as a salary-day surge on a banking app, requires looking at source distribution and request behaviour rather than volume alone.

Mitigation depends on the layer. Volumetric attacks exceed what any single organisation can absorb, so the answer is an upstream scrubbing service or content delivery network that filters traffic before it reaches you, plus ISP blackholing as a last resort. Protocol attacks are addressed with SYN cookies, connection rate limits and firewall tuning. Application attacks need a web application firewall, rate limiting per client, CAPTCHA challenges and caching. On the supply side, network operators should implement BCP 38 ingress filtering so spoofed packets cannot leave their networks, and organisations should not run open resolvers or exposed memcached. On the exam, if a question mentions spoofed source addresses and third-party servers replying to the victim, the answer is reflected; if it mentions small requests producing large responses, the answer is amplified; most real attacks are both.

keyTerms.def: An attack that makes a system or service unavailable by overwhelming or crashing it.
A DoS attack launched simultaneously from many compromised sources, typically a botnet.
A DDoS technique where the attacker spoofs the victim's IP so that third-party servers send their responses to the victim.
A DDoS technique using protocols where a small request produces a much larger response, multiplying the attacker's bandwidth.
A network of compromised devices controlled by an attacker and used collectively, often for DDoS.
A protocol attack that sends many TCP connection requests without completing the handshake, exhausting server connection tables.
An upstream service that absorbs and filters attack traffic before forwarding clean traffic to the target.
The best practice of ingress filtering at network edges so packets with spoofed source addresses are dropped.

examTips: Spoofed source IP plus third-party servers answering to the victim = reflected. Small request, large response = amplified. Real attacks combine both.
DNS, NTP, memcached and SSDP are the amplification protocols the exam names.
For very large volumetric attacks, the answer is an upstream scrubbing or CDN service, not a bigger local firewall.
A single-source flood is DoS; many sources is DDoS. Application-layer attacks can look like legitimate traffic and need rate limiting or a WAF.
videos.realWorld: Nigerian banks and fintechs see DDoS most often as extortion, where a group floods the internet banking portal or USSD gateway and demands payment to stop, or as cover for a fraud attempt elsewhere. A SOC analyst's first job is to confirm it is an attack rather than a marketing campaign or salary-day load, then engage the DDoS protection provider and the ISP. GRC teams make sure the DDoS runbook exists, that the scrubbing contract is current, and that availability incidents are reported in line with CBN incident-reporting timelines.

quiz.q: A company web server is receiving massive volumes of DNS response traffic from hundreds of legitimate DNS servers around the world, even though it never sent any queries. Which attack is this?
quiz.explain: The attacker sent DNS queries with the victim's spoofed source address (reflection) to servers that return large responses (amplification). DNS poisoning corrupts cache records, a SYN flood is a TCP handshake attack, and an on-path attack intercepts traffic.

quiz.q: An online banking portal becomes unresponsive. Logs show a moderate number of requests per second, all targeting the account statement export function with different session cookies and identical user-agent strings. Bandwidth usage is normal. What is the best mitigation?
options: Implement a web application firewall with per-client rate limiting
Enable full-disk encryption on the web server
quiz.explain: This is an application-layer DoS using expensive requests, not a bandwidth flood, so a bigger link would not help. A WAF with rate limiting identifies and throttles the abusive pattern. DNS recursion and disk encryption are unrelated.

quiz.q: Which of the following would most directly reduce an organisation's contribution to reflected DDoS attacks against other networks?
options: Running an open DNS resolver for convenience
Implementing ingress filtering to drop packets with spoofed source addresses
Increasing the size of the firewall state table
quiz.explain: Reflection relies on spoofed source addresses. Ingress filtering (BCP 38) at the network edge drops such packets before they leave. Open resolvers make things worse, while state table size and SYN cookies protect the organisation itself rather than others.

videos.title: DNS Attacks
videos.summary: Messer explains how DNS resolution can be subverted through cache poisoning and domain hijacking, plus related tricks such as URL hijacking and typosquatting.
videos.deepDive:
DNS is the internet's phone book, and almost every connection starts with a lookup. If an attacker controls the answer to where is gtbank.com, they control where the user goes, and the user's browser will show the correct name in the address bar. That is why DNS attacks are so effective and why the exam singles out two: DNS poisoning and domain hijacking.

DNS poisoning (cache poisoning) injects a false record into a resolver's cache so that every client using that resolver receives the wrong IP address until the record expires. The classic method: the attacker sends a query to the target resolver for a name, then floods it with forged responses that guess the transaction ID and source port, hoping one arrives before the legitimate answer. Kaminsky's 2008 research showed how to make this practical by querying random subdomains so the resolver keeps asking. A simpler local version is to modify the hosts file on a workstation, which the OS checks before DNS, or to change the DNS server setting on a home router to an attacker-controlled resolver. Indicators: a known domain resolving to an unexpected IP, especially one in a different country or hosting provider; users landing on certificate warnings for sites that normally have valid certificates; a spike in DNS responses arriving at the resolver that do not match outstanding queries; and hosts-file changes flagged by file integrity monitoring. Mitigation is DNSSEC, which lets resolvers verify signed records, plus randomised source ports and transaction IDs, restricting recursion to internal clients only, and pointing endpoints at hardened corporate resolvers rather than whatever DHCP hands them.

Domain hijacking takes over the domain itself at the registrar. The attacker phishes or brute-forces the registrar account, exploits a registrar flaw, or social-engineers support, then changes the name servers or the A records. Now the whole world, not just one resolver, is directed to the attacker's server, and they can obtain a valid TLS certificate because they genuinely control the domain. In 2019 the Sea Turtle campaign hijacked government and telecom domains this way. Indicators: WHOIS records showing a changed registrant or name server, certificate transparency logs showing a new certificate issued for your domain that you did not request, and customers reporting a different-looking site. Mitigation includes registrar lock, MFA on the registrar account, using a reputable registrar, monitoring WHOIS and certificate transparency, and keeping registration contact details current so renewal notices arrive.

Two related attacks appear in the same video. URL hijacking or typosquatting registers domains close to the real one, such as gtbnak.com or a different top-level domain, hoping users mistype or trust a lookalike in a phishing email. Domain reputation attacks abuse a legitimate domain to send spam or host malware so that it ends up on blocklists and legitimate mail bounces.

Worked example for a SOC: the SIEM correlates DNS logs and finds that 300 internal hosts resolved the corporate VPN hostname to an IP in a hosting provider abroad for 40 minutes. The corporate resolver cache shows the record with an unusual TTL. That is cache poisoning of your own resolver. Triage: flush the cache, check whether any users authenticated to the fake IP (proxy and VPN logs), reset credentials for those users, and enable DNSSEC validation. GRC follow-up: DNS resolver configuration joins the hardening baseline and registrar accounts are added to the privileged-access review.

keyTerms.def: Inserting false records into a DNS resolver cache so clients are directed to attacker-controlled addresses.
Taking control of a domain's registration or DNS settings at the registrar so the domain points to attacker infrastructure globally.
DNS Security Extensions, which digitally sign DNS records so resolvers can verify authenticity and integrity.
Registering domains that are misspellings or lookalikes of legitimate domains to catch mistyped traffic or support phishing.
A registrar setting that prevents domain transfers or name server changes without additional verification.
A local file that maps names to IP addresses and is consulted before DNS, making it a target for local poisoning.
Public logs of issued TLS certificates that can be monitored to detect certificates issued for your domain without authorisation.

examTips: Poisoning affects one resolver's cache; hijacking changes the domain at the registrar and affects everyone. Scope tells you which.
DNSSEC is the answer for preventing poisoning; registrar lock and MFA on the registrar account are the answers for hijacking.
A modified hosts file is a form of local DNS poisoning and is caught by file integrity monitoring.
Typosquatting is the DNS-flavoured social engineering answer when a URL is slightly misspelled.
videos.realWorld: SOC analysts at fintechs pull DNS query logs into the SIEM because they reveal both attacks on DNS and malware using DNS for command and control. A resolver answer that does not match passive DNS history is a fast poisoning indicator. GRC teams register the obvious typosquat variants of the brand, put the registrar account under privileged-access controls, subscribe to certificate transparency monitoring, and keep evidence of these controls for brand-protection and CBN consumer-protection reviews.

quiz.q: Users on one branch network report the internet banking site shows a certificate warning and looks slightly different. Users at other branches are unaffected. The branch uses its own local DNS resolver. What has most likely happened?
options: DNS cache poisoning on the branch resolver
A DDoS against the banking site
quiz.explain: Only clients of one resolver are affected, which points to a poisoned cache on that resolver. Domain hijacking would affect every user globally, a DDoS would cause unavailability rather than a different site, and typosquatting requires users to type a wrong address.

quiz.q: A company discovers that its domain's name servers have been changed at the registrar and a valid TLS certificate for its domain has been issued to an unknown party. Which control would have most directly prevented this?
options: Registrar lock and MFA on the registrar account
quiz.explain: The domain itself was taken over at the registrar, which is domain hijacking. Registrar lock and strong authentication on the registrar account prevent unauthorised changes. DNSSEC and port randomisation defend against cache poisoning, not registrar compromise.

quiz.q: Which technology allows a DNS resolver to verify that a response has not been altered and genuinely comes from the authoritative zone?
quiz.explain: DNSSEC uses digital signatures on records so resolvers can validate origin and integrity. DNS over HTTPS encrypts the transport but does not authenticate the record content, split-horizon serves different answers to different clients, and reverse DNS maps IPs to names.

videos.title: Wireless Attacks
videos.summary: Messer walks through attacks on wireless links: deauthentication and other 802.11 management-frame abuse, radio frequency jamming, and the related short-range technologies RFID and NFC.
videos.deepDive:
Wireless networks share a medium anyone within range can hear and transmit on. That single fact explains every attack in this video. The SY0-701 objective lists evil twin, deauthentication (deauth), RFID and NFC; Messer also covers jamming, which underpins several of them.

Deauthentication abuses 802.11 management frames. In the original standard, the frames that tell a client to disconnect were unauthenticated, so anyone can forge a deauth frame that appears to come from the access point and every client obeys. An attacker uses this to knock a target off the network, either as a plain denial of service or to force the client to reconnect so the attacker can capture the WPA2 four-way handshake and crack the pre-shared key offline. Since 2018, WPA3 and 802.11w Protected Management Frames sign these frames so forged ones are ignored. Indicators: a wireless intrusion detection system reporting bursts of deauth frames, many clients disconnecting simultaneously, and repeated reassociation events in the controller logs. Mitigation is enabling 802.11w or moving to WPA3, which makes it mandatory.

Evil twin is a rogue access point that copies the SSID and often the MAC address of a legitimate one, usually with a stronger signal. Clients that have saved the network auto-connect, and the attacker becomes the gateway for all their traffic. Combined with deauth to push clients off the real AP, it is very reliable in a coffee shop or airport. On an open network the attacker sees everything unencrypted; on a corporate network using WPA2-Enterprise they can capture RADIUS credentials if clients do not validate the server certificate. Indicators: two access points advertising the same SSID with different BSSIDs, an AP appearing in a location where none was installed, and clients reporting certificate warnings when joining. Mitigation: wireless IDS with rogue detection, client configurations that validate the RADIUS server certificate, and user guidance to avoid auto-joining open networks.

Radio frequency jamming floods the frequency with noise so legitimate signals cannot be decoded. It is illegal in most countries, including Nigeria under NCC regulations, but the equipment is cheap. Jamming can be deliberate (a wireless denial of service to force users onto an evil twin) or accidental (a microwave oven or a badly configured neighbouring network). Indicators are a sudden rise in the noise floor and retransmissions on a spectrum analyser. Mitigation is limited to locating the source, changing channels or frequency bands, and using directional antennas.

RFID and NFC attacks target short-range radio. RFID cloning was covered under physical attacks. Additional RFID and NFC attacks include eavesdropping on a legitimate transaction with a high-gain antenna, relay attacks where two attackers extend the range of a card in a victim's pocket to a reader metres away, and data manipulation on writable tags. Contactless payment cards are the prime target, which is why they enforce low transaction limits, generate a unique cryptogram per transaction, and why relay attacks are countered by timing checks. Indicators are transaction patterns: the same card used in two places moments apart, or low-value transactions clustered at an unusual merchant.

Worked example for a SOC: the wireless controller reports a new BSSID broadcasting the corporate SSID from the car park, followed by a burst of deauth frames and 30 laptops reassociating. Five of them attempted to join the rogue and one user entered domain credentials into a captive portal. Triage: locate and remove the rogue, reset that user's credentials, check for logins with those credentials from unexpected sources, and confirm 802.11w and server certificate validation are enforced in the client profile.

keyTerms.def: Sending forged 802.11 deauth management frames to disconnect clients from a wireless network.
A rogue access point that imitates a legitimate network's SSID to lure clients and intercept their traffic.
A Wi-Fi standard that authenticates management frames so forged deauth and disassociation frames are ignored; mandatory in WPA3.
Transmitting noise on a frequency to prevent legitimate wireless communication, a wireless denial of service.
Any access point connected to a network without authorisation, whether installed by an attacker or a careless employee.
Extending the range of a contactless card by relaying its signal between two attacker devices so it can be used at a distant reader.
A system that monitors the airspace for rogue access points, deauth floods and other wireless attacks.
The WPA2 exchange that establishes session keys, which can be captured during reconnection and attacked offline to recover the pre-shared key.

examTips: Many clients disconnecting at once and reconnecting = deauth attack; the fix is 802.11w or WPA3.
Same SSID from an unexpected access point, often with a stronger signal, = evil twin.
Jamming is a wireless denial of service; the exam answer for detecting it is a spectrum analyser.
Contactless card used in two locations minutes apart suggests NFC relay or cloning; per-transaction cryptograms and limits reduce the damage.
videos.realWorld: Banks with branch Wi-Fi and fintechs with open-plan offices run wireless intrusion detection because a rogue AP is the easiest way for an attacker to get inside the perimeter without touching a cable. SOC analysts watch for rogue BSSIDs and deauth bursts and coordinate with facilities to physically find the device. On the payments side, fraud and SOC teams share indicators for contactless relay and cloning, and GRC ensures that client Wi-Fi profiles enforce certificate validation and that the wireless standard is part of the network security policy reviewed at audit.

quiz.q: Employees in a branch report that their laptops keep dropping off Wi-Fi every few minutes and then reconnecting. The wireless controller shows a flood of disconnection management frames not sent by any managed access point. Which attack is occurring and what is the best fix?
options: Deauthentication attack; enable Protected Management Frames or migrate to WPA3
NFC relay; lower the transaction limit
quiz.explain: Forged disconnection frames causing repeated drops is a deauthentication attack. 802.11w Protected Management Frames, mandatory in WPA3, authenticate those frames so forged ones are ignored. Hiding the SSID does nothing, jamming would show as noise rather than frames, and NFC is unrelated.

quiz.q: A wireless IDS detects an access point broadcasting the corporate SSID from outside the building with a different BSSID. Several users then received a certificate warning when connecting. What is this and what control would have protected the users' credentials?
options: Rogue evil twin; configure clients to validate the RADIUS server certificate
quiz.explain: A second AP mimicking the SSID is an evil twin. When clients are configured to validate the authentication server certificate, they refuse to send credentials to a rogue that presents an untrusted certificate. The other options address different attacks.

quiz.q: A customer's contactless card was used at a shop in Ibadan and, 90 seconds later, at a shop in Lagos. The card is still in the customer's possession. Which attack best explains this?
quiz.explain: Using a contactless card at two distant readers within a short time while the card remains with the owner points to an NFC relay attack, where the card's signal is forwarded to a remote reader, or to cloning. Wireless LAN and DNS attacks do not explain payment transactions.

videos.title: On-path Attacks
videos.summary: Messer describes on-path (formerly man-in-the-middle) attacks in which the attacker sits between two parties and reads or alters their traffic, using ARP poisoning and on-path browser attacks as examples.
videos.deepDive:
An on-path attack places the attacker logically between two communicating parties so that traffic flows through the attacker's system. Both sides believe they are talking directly to each other. The attacker can passively read everything or actively modify it: change a bank account number in a transfer, inject a script into a web page, or strip encryption. CompTIA now uses on-path rather than man-in-the-middle, but you will see both terms in practice.

The most common local technique is ARP poisoning (ARP spoofing). On an IPv4 LAN, hosts find each other's MAC addresses with ARP, and ARP has no authentication. The attacker broadcasts forged ARP replies telling the victim that the gateway's IP maps to the attacker's MAC, and telling the gateway that the victim's IP maps to the attacker's MAC. Both update their ARP caches. From then on, the switch delivers the victim's outbound traffic to the attacker, who forwards it to the real gateway after reading or editing it. Tools such as Ettercap or Bettercap automate this in seconds. Indicators: two IP addresses mapped to the same MAC in ARP tables, a flurry of gratuitous ARP replies captured on the segment, switch logs from Dynamic ARP Inspection showing dropped packets, and a host that suddenly starts forwarding traffic it should not. Mitigation: Dynamic ARP Inspection and DHCP snooping on managed switches, static ARP entries for critical hosts, network segmentation, and above all end-to-end encryption so intercepted traffic is unreadable.

Other on-path positions include a rogue Wi-Fi access point (the evil twin from the previous video), a compromised router or ISP link, a malicious proxy configured through a WPAD or PAC file, and DNS poisoning that sends users to the attacker's server. In every case the attacker aims to be the hop the traffic must cross.

On-path browser attacks (man-in-the-browser) work differently. Instead of intercepting packets on the network, malware such as a malicious browser extension or a trojan like Zeus hooks the browser itself. It sees the page after decryption and before display, so TLS offers no protection. The malware can show the user a legitimate-looking transfer confirmation while sending different instructions to the bank, and it can rewrite the balance shown afterwards so the theft is hidden. The user, the browser padlock and the bank's server all report everything is fine. Indicators are behavioural: transactions the customer denies making from a device that otherwise looks legitimate, injected form fields asking for extra data such as a full card PIN, and unusual DLL or extension loads in the browser process. Mitigation: endpoint protection, browser extension control, and, on the bank side, transaction signing or out-of-band confirmation of the payee and amount on a separate device, which is why Nigerian banks send transaction details by SMS or app notification for approval.

How TLS fits in. Properly deployed TLS defeats most network on-path attacks because the attacker cannot present a certificate the browser trusts for the real domain. Attacks therefore try to avoid TLS: SSL stripping downgrades the connection to HTTP when the user types a bare domain, which HSTS prevents; and installing a rogue root certificate on the victim makes the attacker's certificate trusted, which is why corporate devices restrict who can add certificates.

Worked SOC example: an analyst at a Lagos fintech sees an IDS alert for ARP spoofing on the operations VLAN. The switch's Dynamic ARP Inspection log shows a workstation sending replies claiming to be the gateway. The analyst isolates that port, images the workstation, and finds Bettercap running under a contractor's account. Follow-up: review what traffic crossed that segment during the window, reset credentials for services that were not using TLS, and add DAI to the segments that lacked it.

keyTerms.def: An attack where the adversary positions themselves between two parties to intercept, read or alter their communication; formerly called man-in-the-middle.
Sending forged ARP replies to associate the attacker's MAC address with another host's IP so LAN traffic is redirected through the attacker.
Malware inside the browser that reads and modifies web sessions after decryption, defeating TLS; also called man-in-the-browser.
A switch feature that validates ARP packets against DHCP snooping bindings and drops forged replies.
An on-path downgrade that forces a client onto plain HTTP instead of HTTPS so traffic can be read.
HTTP Strict Transport Security, a header instructing browsers to use HTTPS only for a domain, preventing SSL stripping.
An unsolicited ARP reply announcing an IP-to-MAC mapping, legitimate in some cases but abused for poisoning.

examTips: Two different IPs mapped to one MAC, or a device claiming to be the gateway, = ARP poisoning; the switch fix is Dynamic ARP Inspection.
If TLS is in place and the user still sees altered transactions, the attack is in the browser, not the network.
End-to-end encryption is the general answer for making on-path interception useless; HSTS is the specific answer for SSL stripping.
The exam uses on-path, not man-in-the-middle, in question stems and answers.
videos.realWorld: For fraud and SOC teams in banking, man-in-the-browser trojans on customer devices are a recurring cause of disputed transfers, which is why transaction-signing and out-of-band confirmation exist. Inside the enterprise, ARP spoofing alerts from switches or from tools like arpwatch are a strong signal that someone is running attack tooling on the LAN. GRC analysts verify that DAI and DHCP snooping are part of the switch hardening standard and that internal services, not just internet-facing ones, use TLS, because auditors and CBN examiners now ask about encryption in transit for internal traffic too.

quiz.q: An intrusion detection sensor reports that a workstation on the finance VLAN is sending ARP replies claiming the default gateway's IP address. Shortly afterwards, several finance users complain of slow connections. What is happening?
options: An ARP poisoning on-path attack redirecting traffic through the workstation
A DDoS attack against the gateway
quiz.explain: Forged ARP replies impersonating the gateway cause other hosts to send traffic to the attacker, who forwards it after inspection; the extra hop causes the slowdown. DDoS would flood rather than redirect, DNS poisoning does not involve ARP, and deauth is a wireless attack.

quiz.q: A bank customer insists she transferred 50,000 naira to a friend, but the bank's logs show 500,000 naira sent to an unknown account, and the padlock and balance shown in her browser appeared normal. The connection used TLS. What best explains this?
options: SSL stripping on the coffee shop Wi-Fi
An on-path browser attack modifying the transaction inside the browser
quiz.explain: Because TLS was intact and the displayed page was manipulated, the tampering happened inside the browser after decryption, which is a man-in-the-browser attack. SSL stripping would have removed HTTPS, hijacking would send her to a different site, and replay reuses captured data rather than altering a live session.

quiz.q: Which switch configuration most directly prevents ARP poisoning on an access VLAN?
options: Dynamic ARP Inspection with DHCP snooping
quiz.explain: Dynamic ARP Inspection checks ARP packets against the trusted IP-to-MAC bindings learned by DHCP snooping and drops forged replies. Port mirroring copies traffic for monitoring, jumbo frames concern packet size, and Spanning Tree prevents loops.

videos.title: Replay Attacks
videos.summary: Messer explains replay attacks, where captured authentication data or session tokens are resent to impersonate a user, with pass-the-hash and session hijacking as the key examples.
videos.deepDive:
A replay attack reuses valid data that the attacker captured earlier. The attacker does not need to decrypt or crack anything; they simply send the same bytes again and hope the receiving system accepts them a second time. The objective lists credential replay as an indicator of malicious activity and replay under application attacks, so expect it from both angles.

The attack has three steps. First, capture: the attacker obtains the data through an on-path position, a compromised host, malware, or by reading it from memory or disk. Second, wait or act immediately, depending on how long the data stays valid. Third, replay: present the captured data to the server as if it were original. The system is vulnerable whenever it cannot distinguish a fresh message from a copy.

Pass-the-hash is the textbook credential replay in Windows environments. NTLM authentication proves knowledge of the password hash, not the password, so the hash itself is effectively the credential. An attacker with local admin on one workstation dumps hashes from memory using a tool such as Mimikatz, then uses them to authenticate to file shares, other workstations or servers, without ever knowing the plaintext password. This is a primary lateral-movement technique in ransomware intrusions. Indicators: Windows Security Event 4624 logons with logon type 3 (network) and authentication package NTLM from a workstation to many hosts, especially using a privileged account; Event 4776 NTLM validation spikes; and EDR alerts for LSASS memory access (Sysmon Event 10). Mitigation: Kerberos in preference to NTLM, Credential Guard to protect LSASS, restricting local admin rights, LAPS so local admin passwords differ per machine, and tiered administration so domain admin credentials are never present on workstations.

Session hijacking (cookie or token replay) targets web applications. After login, the browser holds a session cookie that proves identity on every request. If the attacker steals it, through cross-site scripting, malware, an unencrypted network, or a misconfigured proxy, they can paste it into their own browser and are logged in as the victim with no password and no MFA prompt, because MFA was completed when the session was created. Modern phishing kits such as Evilginx operate as a reverse proxy to capture the cookie at login time, which is why they defeat SMS and app-based MFA but not FIDO2 keys bound to the origin. Indicators: the same session ID used from two IP addresses or two user agents, a session that continues after the user's device went offline, and geolocation jumps within one session. Mitigation: mark cookies Secure and HttpOnly, bind sessions to client attributes, expire sessions promptly, rotate the session ID after login, and use phishing-resistant MFA.

The general cure for replay is to make every message unique and time-bound. A nonce (number used once) is issued by the server and must be included in the response; a replayed message carries an old nonce and is rejected. Timestamps with a short validity window and sequence numbers do the same job. Kerberos uses timestamped authenticators, TLS includes random values from both sides in every handshake, and payment cryptograms include a transaction counter. When a question asks how to defend against replay, look for nonce, timestamp, sequence number or session token rotation among the choices.

Worked SOC example: the SIEM flags a service account with NTLM network logons to 45 servers in ten minutes from a call-centre workstation. That account should only run on two application servers. The analyst treats this as pass-the-hash lateral movement, isolates the workstation, forces a password reset on the account (and any other accounts that logged onto that workstation), and checks the 45 servers for follow-on activity.

keyTerms.def: Capturing valid transmitted data such as credentials or tokens and resending it later to gain unauthorised access.
Authenticating with a stolen NTLM password hash instead of the plaintext password, commonly used for lateral movement in Windows networks.
Taking over an authenticated web session by stealing and reusing the victim's session cookie or token.
A random number used once in a protocol exchange so that any replayed message can be recognised and rejected.
A Windows feature that isolates LSASS secrets in a virtualised container so tools like Mimikatz cannot dump hashes.
An attacker moving from one compromised system to others within the network, often by reusing captured credentials.
Authentication such as FIDO2 security keys that binds the credential to the legitimate site so a proxied login cannot be replayed.

examTips: Replay does not require decryption; if the scenario says the attacker reused captured data without cracking it, it is replay.
Pass-the-hash indicators are NTLM network logons from one host to many others; the fixes are Kerberos, Credential Guard and removing local admin rights.
Nonces, timestamps and sequence numbers are the classic anti-replay answers.
A stolen session cookie bypasses MFA because authentication already happened; the fix is short-lived, rotated, Secure and HttpOnly cookies.
videos.realWorld: Pass-the-hash is the lateral-movement technique SOC analysts at banks see most in real intrusions, and detection rules for NTLM fan-out and LSASS access are standard in mature SIEM deployments. On the customer-facing side, session token theft through reverse-proxy phishing kits has become the main way criminals defeat OTP-based MFA on Nigerian banking apps, pushing fintechs toward device binding and app-based push confirmations. GRC teams push for tiered admin models, LAPS and Credential Guard as documented controls, and track session-timeout settings as part of application security standards.

quiz.q: An attacker captures a user's session cookie over an unencrypted Wi-Fi network and uses it in their own browser to access the user's account without being asked for a password or MFA code. What type of attack is this?
quiz.explain: Reusing a captured session token to impersonate an authenticated user is session hijacking, a form of replay. No guessing occurred (brute force), no protocol weakening (downgrade), and no file system access (traversal).

quiz.q: Security logs show NTLM network logons by a domain administrator account from a single help-desk workstation to over 50 servers within a few minutes. No interactive logon by that administrator occurred on the workstation. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Pass-the-hash lateral movement using a stolen credential hash
A logic bomb has been triggered
The administrator is running a scheduled inventory script
quiz.explain: Authentication via NTLM to many hosts from an unexpected source without an interactive logon is the pattern of pass-the-hash, where the attacker reuses a dumped hash. DNS poisoning and logic bombs do not produce authentication fan-out.

quiz.q: A developer wants to ensure that an intercepted authentication message cannot be reused later to log in. Which mechanism should the protocol include?
options: A server-issued nonce or timestamp that must be included in each response
quiz.explain: A nonce or timestamp makes each authentication exchange unique so a replayed message is rejected. Password length, encoding and key size do not stop a valid captured message from being resent.

videos.title: Malicious Code
videos.summary: Messer describes malicious code as the broad category of scripts, macros, executables and injected commands used to compromise systems, and how it is delivered and detected.
videos.deepDive:
The objective lists malicious code as a network-and-application indicator, separate from malware. The distinction is deliberate. Malware is a packaged program with a family name; malicious code is any code, in any form, that an attacker gets a system to execute. That includes a one-line PowerShell command in a phishing email, a JavaScript snippet injected into a web page, a macro in a spreadsheet, a shell script left in a cron job, a modified npm package, or a SQL fragment that turns a login form into a data dump. Many of these never touch disk as a file that antivirus would recognise, which is exactly why they are useful to attackers.

Think about malicious code in terms of where it runs. Client-side code runs on the user's machine: macros, scripts, browser exploits and malicious extensions. Server-side code runs on your infrastructure: web shells uploaded through a file upload flaw, injected commands via SQL or OS command injection, and backdoors added to application source or dependencies. Network-delivered code arrives as an exploit payload against a listening service and runs with that service's privileges.

Common delivery paths a SOC will actually see. Phishing with script attachments: an HTML, JS, VBS, LNK or ISO file that, when opened, runs a script to download the real payload; Windows Script Host and mshta.exe are the usual interpreters. Macros in Office files. Web shells: a PHP, ASPX or JSP file uploaded to a web server that gives the attacker a command prompt through their browser; ProxyShell and the 2021 Exchange attacks left thousands of these. Cross-site scripting: JavaScript injected into a page runs in every visitor's browser. Supply chain: a malicious update or dependency, as in SolarWinds or the many typosquatted PyPI packages. Living off the land: attackers avoid bringing their own binaries and instead use PowerShell, certutil, bitsadmin, wmic and rundll32 that are already present and signed by Microsoft.

Indicators in logs. Process creation events where a document reader or browser spawns an interpreter: winword.exe to powershell.exe, outlook.exe to wscript.exe. Command lines with -EncodedCommand, -nop -w hidden, IEX, DownloadString, or long Base64 strings. PowerShell Script Block Logging (Event 4104) showing decoded content. New files in web directories with recent timestamps that do not match the deployment. Web server logs showing POST requests to a file that was never part of the application. Scheduled tasks or cron entries pointing at unusual locations. Outbound connections from processes that should not need the internet.

Worked example: an analyst at a Nigerian payment switch sees Event 4104 on an application server containing a decoded script that downloads a file from a Discord CDN link and sets a scheduled task. The parent process was an IIS worker process. That combination, web server spawning PowerShell, is a web shell in action. Triage: pull the web logs to find the upload path and the attacker's IP, image the server, identify the uploaded shell, check other servers for the same file hash, block the download URL, and patch the upload vulnerability.

Mitigation is about limiting what code can run and watching what does. Application allow listing (Windows Defender Application Control or AppLocker) blocks unapproved executables and scripts. Constrained Language Mode and execution policies limit PowerShell. Attack surface reduction rules stop Office from spawning child processes. Mail gateways strip active content and block risky attachment types. Web application firewalls and input validation stop injection. Secure development and dependency scanning address supply chain code. And script block logging plus EDR make the code visible when prevention fails.

keyTerms.def: Any script, macro, command or program fragment that an attacker causes a system to execute, whether or not it is packaged as a recognisable malware file.
A script uploaded to a web server that lets an attacker execute commands on the server through a browser.
Legitimate, signed system tools such as PowerShell, certutil and mshta that attackers use to run malicious code without dropping their own executables.
A PowerShell logging feature (Event ID 4104) that records the decoded content of executed script blocks.
A control that permits only approved executables and scripts to run, blocking everything else by default.
Windows Defender policies that block risky behaviours such as Office applications creating child processes.
Inserting malicious code into a software update, library or dependency so that it is distributed and trusted as legitimate.

examTips: Malicious code is broader than malware; a scenario about a script, macro or injected command that runs is malicious code even if no file was saved.
Office or a browser spawning PowerShell, wscript or cmd is the signature indicator the exam expects you to recognise.
A newly created file in a web server directory that accepts commands via HTTP = web shell.
Application allow listing is the strongest preventive answer; script block logging and EDR are the detective answers.
videos.realWorld: SOC detection engineering at fintechs is largely about malicious code: rules for encoded PowerShell, suspicious parent-child process chains, LOLBin abuse and web shell behaviour catch far more real intrusions than file-hash matching. Analysts learn to decode Base64 command lines quickly and to recognise the handful of download-and-execute patterns that recur. GRC contributes by mandating allow listing on servers that handle card data, logging standards that include script block logging, and secure development practices with dependency scanning in the SDLC, all of which map to PCI DSS and CBN application security expectations.

quiz.q: PowerShell Script Block Logging on a web server records a decoded script that downloads a file from an external URL and creates a scheduled task. The parent process of PowerShell was the IIS worker process. What has most likely occurred?
