options: A web shell is being used to execute malicious code on the server
quiz.explain: A web server process spawning PowerShell to download and persist a payload indicates an attacker executing commands through a web shell. Legitimate administrators do not run updates through IIS, and wireless or DNS flood attacks do not produce this process chain.

quiz.q: An organisation wants to prevent unapproved scripts and executables from running on its servers, regardless of whether antivirus recognises them. Which control best meets this requirement?
quiz.explain: Application allow listing blocks any executable or script not explicitly approved, which defeats novel malicious code that signatures would miss. Antivirus relies on recognition, disk encryption protects data at rest, and a network firewall does not control local execution.

quiz.q: An email attachment named statement.html opens a page that immediately launches wscript.exe with a downloaded file. Which description best fits this activity?
options: Client-side malicious code delivered by phishing
quiz.explain: A script inside an HTML attachment that invokes the Windows Script Host to fetch and run a payload is malicious code executing on the client, delivered through phishing. The other options describe unrelated categories.

videos.title: Application Attacks
videos.summary: Messer covers attacks aimed at application logic and memory: injection, buffer overflow, replay, privilege escalation, forgery (CSRF and SSRF) and directory traversal.
videos.deepDive:
Application attacks exploit the way software handles input. Almost every one on this list comes down to the same root cause: the application trusted data it received from a user or another system and did something dangerous with it. The exam expects you to identify the attack from a short scenario and to know the primary fix.

Injection inserts attacker-supplied data into a command the application builds. In SQL injection, a login form that concatenates input into SELECT * FROM users WHERE name=' plus the input lets an attacker type ' OR '1'='1 to make the condition always true, or append a UNION SELECT to read other tables. Command injection does the same with operating-system commands, LDAP injection with directory queries, and XML injection with XML documents. Indicators: web logs containing quotes, comment sequences such as -- or /*, keywords like UNION or SLEEP, or shell metacharacters like ; and |; database errors returned to clients; and a spike in 500 errors followed by a large data response. Mitigation: parameterised queries (prepared statements) so input can never become code, input validation, least-privilege database accounts, and a WAF as a second layer.

Buffer overflow is a memory attack. A program allocates a fixed-size buffer and copies input into it without checking length. Excess input overwrites adjacent memory, including the return address on the stack, so the attacker can redirect execution to their own code. Indicators are application crashes with access violations, unusually long inputs in logs, and EDR exploit-protection alerts. Mitigation: safe languages or bounds-checked functions, and OS defences such as ASLR, DEP/NX and stack canaries, plus patching.

Privilege escalation is the attacker moving from lower to higher rights. Vertical escalation goes from user to admin or SYSTEM, usually by exploiting a kernel or service vulnerability or a misconfiguration such as a writable service binary. Horizontal escalation accesses another user's data at the same level, such as changing an account ID in a URL to see someone else's statement, an insecure direct object reference. Indicators: Event 4672 special privileges assigned to a normal user, new local admin group members (Event 4732), processes running as SYSTEM launched from a user session, and sudo entries in Linux auth logs for users who should not have them. Mitigation: patching, least privilege, removing local admin, and server-side authorisation checks on every request.

Forgery covers two attacks. Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending a request the user did not intend, such as a hidden form that transfers money, because the browser attaches the session cookie automatically. The fix is anti-CSRF tokens tied to the session and SameSite cookie attributes. Server-side request forgery (SSRF) makes the server fetch a URL the attacker chooses, often an internal address like a cloud metadata endpoint at 169.254.169.254, turning the server into a proxy into the internal network. The fix is strict allow lists for outbound URLs and blocking internal ranges.

Directory traversal uses ../ sequences in a file path parameter to escape the intended folder and read files such as /etc/passwd or web.config. Look for ../ or its URL-encoded form %2e%2e%2f in web logs. The fix is canonicalising paths, validating against an allow list, and running the web server with minimal file permissions.

Replay in the application context was covered in the previous video: reusing a captured token or request. The fix is nonces, timestamps and short-lived, rotated session tokens.

Worked SOC example: a WAF at a Nigerian fintech alerts on requests to /api/statement?file=../../../../etc/passwd followed by a 200 response of 2 KB. That is a successful traversal. The analyst confirms the response content, blocks the source, checks what other files were requested, and raises a critical ticket to the application team, because the same flaw probably exposes configuration files with database credentials.

keyTerms.def: Inserting SQL syntax through user input so that the application executes attacker-controlled database commands.
A database query with placeholders for input values so user data is never interpreted as SQL code; the primary defence against injection.
Writing more data into a memory buffer than it can hold, overwriting adjacent memory and potentially redirecting program execution.
Gaining higher rights than authorised, either vertically to admin level or horizontally to another user's resources.
Causing a logged-in user's browser to submit an unintended request to a site that trusts the user's session.
Making a server issue requests to attacker-chosen URLs, often to reach internal systems the attacker cannot access directly.
Using ../ path sequences in input to access files outside the web application's intended directory.
Operating system protections that randomise memory layout and mark data regions non-executable to make buffer overflow exploitation harder.

examTips: Quotes, OR 1=1, UNION or comment markers in input = SQL injection; the fix is parameterised queries and input validation.
../ or %2e%2e%2f in a URL = directory traversal.
CSRF exploits the victim's browser and session; SSRF exploits the server's ability to make requests. Read carefully for which side is being forged.
Application crash on a very long input = buffer overflow; answers include input length checking, ASLR, DEP and patching.
A normal user suddenly holding admin rights or accessing another user's records = privilege escalation.
videos.realWorld: SOC analysts at fintechs triage WAF alerts every day, and the skill is distinguishing a scanner spraying payloads (thousands of injection strings, all returning 403) from a targeted attack that got a 200 with data. Web logs, response sizes and status codes tell the story. GRC and application security teams require secure coding standards, code review and penetration testing before release, run vulnerability scans against production, and track remediation of injection and traversal findings because PCI DSS 6.x and CBN application security expectations explicitly call for them.

quiz.q: A web server log shows a request to a page with the parameter user=admin' OR '1'='1 followed by a large response. Which attack is this and what is the primary fix?
options: SQL injection; use parameterised queries and input validation
quiz.explain: The quote and always-true OR clause is classic SQL injection. Parameterised queries ensure input cannot alter query structure. The other attacks and fixes do not match the payload.

quiz.q: A customer logged into an online banking site visits a malicious page in another tab. Without any further action by the customer, a request is sent from her browser that changes the email address on her bank account. What attack does this describe?
quiz.explain: The malicious page caused the victim's own browser to send an authenticated request to a site she was logged into, which is CSRF. SSRF would involve the server making a request, replay reuses captured data, and escalation involves gaining higher rights.

quiz.q: Logs show a standard user account on a file server executed a process that created a new member of the local Administrators group. No administrator performed this action. What has occurred?
quiz.explain: A low-privilege account gaining administrative rights is vertical privilege escalation, typically via an exploit or misconfiguration. The remaining options are unrelated network or file-path attacks.

videos.title: Cryptographic Attacks
videos.summary: Messer explains attacks that target cryptography rather than break it outright: downgrade attacks that force weaker algorithms, and collision and birthday attacks against hash functions.
videos.deepDive:
Modern ciphers are not broken by brute force; AES-256 and RSA-2048 are far beyond any realistic computation. Cryptographic attacks therefore aim at how cryptography is used: persuading systems to use something weaker, or exploiting mathematical properties of hash functions. The objective names three: downgrade, collision and birthday.

A downgrade attack forces two parties to negotiate a weaker protocol or cipher than they both support. Protocol negotiation is the weak point. When a client and server agree on TLS, they exchange lists of supported versions and cipher suites. An on-path attacker who can tamper with that exchange can make each side believe the other only supports an old version. POODLE in 2014 exploited this to force SSL 3.0, then used a known weakness in that version to decrypt cookies. FREAK and Logjam forced export-grade 512-bit keys that could be factored in hours. SSL stripping is a downgrade from HTTPS to HTTP entirely. Downgrade attacks also exist in Wi-Fi, where an attacker forces WPA2 instead of WPA3 in transition mode, and in Windows authentication, where NTLMv1 can be negotiated instead of Kerberos. Indicators: TLS handshakes negotiating versions or ciphers that your policy has deprecated (visible in load balancer or web server logs and in TLS inspection data), unexpected fallback events, and clients connecting with SSLv3 or RC4 when the client population should not need them. Mitigation is straightforward: disable the weak options entirely so there is nothing to downgrade to, enforce minimum TLS 1.2, use HSTS, and enable TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV so a client can signal that a fallback was not its choice.

A collision is two different inputs producing the same hash. Hashes are supposed to be unique fingerprints, so a collision lets an attacker substitute one document for another while the signature still verifies. MD5 collisions have been practical since 2004; the Flame malware in 2012 used an MD5 collision to forge a Microsoft code-signing certificate. SHA-1 fell in 2017 when the SHAttered attack produced two different PDFs with the same SHA-1 hash. Both are now unacceptable for signatures and certificates; SHA-256 or better is the standard. Indicators are indirect: a file whose hash matches a known good value but whose content or behaviour differs, or certificates and signatures still using MD5 or SHA-1.

The birthday attack is the mathematics that makes collisions easier than intuition suggests. The birthday paradox says that in a room of only 23 people there is a 50 percent chance two share a birthday, because you are comparing every pair, not one person against the rest. Applied to hashes, finding any two inputs that collide needs roughly 2 to the power of n/2 attempts for an n-bit hash, not 2 to the power of n. A 128-bit hash like MD5 therefore offers only about 64 bits of collision resistance, which is within reach. This is why hash outputs need to be long, and why the exam links birthday attacks to collisions and to the choice of SHA-256 over shorter hashes.

Worked example: a Nigerian bank's certificate inventory shows an internal payment gateway still using a SHA-1 signed certificate issued by the internal CA and accepting TLS 1.0. A penetration tester demonstrates a downgrade to TLS 1.0 with a CBC cipher and explains that a forged SHA-1 certificate is now feasible. For a SOC analyst, the immediate action is to check whether any external client actually negotiated those weak parameters. For GRC, the finding becomes a cryptographic standard: minimum TLS 1.2, SHA-256 signatures, an inventory of certificates and algorithms, and a crypto-agility plan so the next deprecated algorithm can be retired quickly.

Contrast to remember: a downgrade attack targets negotiation and needs an on-path position; collision and birthday attacks target the hash function and do not need to intercept anything. Neither breaks a properly configured modern cipher; both exploit legacy support that someone forgot to switch off.

keyTerms.def: Forcing a connection to use an older or weaker protocol version or cipher suite that has known weaknesses.
Two different inputs that produce the same hash output, undermining the hash's use as a unique fingerprint.
A method that exploits the birthday paradox to find hash collisions in roughly 2^(n/2) attempts for an n-bit hash.
A 2014 attack that downgraded TLS connections to SSL 3.0 in order to exploit its padding weakness.
A downgrade that converts an HTTPS connection to HTTP, prevented by HSTS.
The 2017 demonstration of a practical SHA-1 collision using two different PDF files.
A signalling cipher suite value that lets a client indicate a protocol fallback so servers can reject forced downgrades.
The ability to replace cryptographic algorithms and keys quickly when they are deprecated.

examTips: Downgrade = negotiation forced to something weaker; the fix is to disable weak protocols and ciphers and enforce a minimum version.
Collision = two inputs, same hash; birthday attack = the reason collisions are found faster than expected. Both point to MD5 and SHA-1 being unsafe.
If the question asks which hash to use to resist collisions, choose SHA-256 or longer.
HSTS is the specific answer for SSL stripping, which is a downgrade attack.
videos.realWorld: Cryptographic attack questions become certificate and configuration hygiene in practice. SOC analysts review TLS logs for deprecated protocol negotiation and investigate certificate anomalies, while GRC teams maintain the cryptographic standard, the certificate inventory and the deprecation schedule that PCI DSS, CBN and NDPA-aligned assessments expect. Weak TLS on internet-facing banking endpoints shows up in external attack-surface scans and is a common audit finding at Nigerian institutions.

quiz.q: A penetration tester demonstrates that by intercepting the TLS handshake she can make a client and server use SSL 3.0 with an RC4 cipher, even though both support TLS 1.3. What type of attack is this and what is the best remediation?
options: Downgrade attack; disable SSL 3.0, weak ciphers and enforce a minimum TLS version
quiz.explain: Forcing a weaker protocol during negotiation is a downgrade attack. Removing the weak options from the server configuration leaves nothing to downgrade to. The other options address hashing or replay, not negotiation.

quiz.q: Two different files are found to produce the identical MD5 hash, and one of them has been substituted for a signed installer without invalidating the signature. Which concept does this demonstrate?
quiz.explain: Two inputs with the same hash is a collision, which lets an attacker swap content while a hash-based signature still verifies. The other options are unrelated to hash properties.

quiz.q: Why is a 128-bit hash considered to provide only about 64 bits of protection against an attacker trying to find any two colliding inputs?
options: Because hashes are truncated in transit
Because half the bits are used for padding
Because of the birthday paradox, collisions are expected after roughly 2^64 attempts
Because MD5 is encrypted with a 64-bit key
quiz.explain: The birthday attack shows that finding any collision requires about the square root of the total output space, so an n-bit hash resists collisions only to about n/2 bits. The other statements are not true of hash functions.

videos.title: Password Attacks
videos.summary: Messer explains how attackers recover or guess passwords: password spraying across many accounts, brute force online and offline, and the role of hashing, salting and lockout policies.
videos.deepDive:
Passwords are still the most common credential, so attacks on them are the most common attacks a SOC sees. The objective names two: spraying and brute force. To understand both you need the distinction between online and offline attacks, and what a hash and a salt do.

An online attack sends guesses to the live system: a login page, VPN portal, RDP, SSH or Microsoft 365. It is limited by network speed, rate limiting and account lockout, and every attempt generates a log entry. An offline attack works on a stolen copy of password hashes, from a breached database, a dumped Active Directory ntds.dit, or a captured Wi-Fi handshake. The attacker can make billions of guesses per second on GPUs with no logs at all, and the only defence is a strong hash algorithm and strong passwords.

Brute force tries every possible combination. Against an 8-character lowercase password, that is about 200 billion possibilities, which a modern GPU rig exhausts against a fast hash like NTLM or MD5 in minutes. Add length and character variety and the space grows exponentially, which is why length is the single best defence. A dictionary attack is a smarter brute force: it tries words, common passwords and known-breach passwords first, with rules that append years and swap letters for digits. Rainbow tables precompute hashes for many passwords so cracking becomes a lookup; salting defeats them, because a random salt per user means the same password hashes differently and tables would have to be built per salt. Slow, memory-hard hashes such as bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2 or PBKDF2 with a high iteration count make each guess expensive, which is what the exam means by key stretching.

Password spraying flips the brute-force approach. Instead of many guesses against one account, which triggers lockout, the attacker tries one or two very common passwords, such as Password2024! or Company@123, against every account in the organisation, then waits past the lockout observation window and tries the next password. Any large organisation has someone using a password like that. Spraying is the dominant technique against cloud portals and VPNs because lockout policies do not see it as an attack.

Indicators for each are distinct. Brute force online: many failed logons (Windows Event 4625, Linux Failed password in auth.log) for one account from one source in a short window, often followed by Event 4740 account lockout. Spraying: a small number of failures for a large number of different accounts from the same source IP or from a rotating pool of IPs, spread evenly over time; in Azure AD or Entra sign-in logs it appears as many users with error code 50126 from one IP. Offline attacks produce no authentication logs at all; the indicator is the theft that preceded them, such as access to ntds.dit, a domain controller backup, or LSASS memory.

Worked SOC example: over four hours, one external IP produces exactly two failed logons for each of 1,200 accounts on a Nigerian bank's Office 365 tenant, then succeeds on three. That is spraying. The analyst blocks the IP, resets the three compromised accounts, revokes their sessions, checks for mailbox rules and MFA registration changes on those accounts (common follow-on actions), and reviews conditional access policy to require MFA and block legacy authentication, which is how sprayers avoid MFA.

Mitigation, in exam order of preference: MFA, which makes a guessed password insufficient; lockout and rate limiting for online brute force; smart lockout and impossible-travel detection for spraying; banned-password lists and length-based policy; salting and slow hashing for stored passwords; and monitoring of authentication logs. Password managers help because they let users hold long unique passwords they never have to remember.

keyTerms.def: Systematically trying every possible password until the correct one is found, either online against a live system or offline against stolen hashes.
Trying one or a few common passwords against many accounts to avoid triggering per-account lockout.
A brute-force variant that tries likely passwords from word lists and breach data before exhaustive search.
Random data added to each password before hashing so identical passwords produce different hashes and precomputed tables are useless.
Using a deliberately slow hash such as bcrypt, PBKDF2 or Argon2 so each password guess costs significant computation.
A precomputed table of password hashes used to reverse unsalted hashes quickly.
A policy that disables an account after a set number of failed attempts, effective against brute force but not spraying.
Older protocols such as basic auth for IMAP or SMTP that do not support MFA and are favoured targets for spraying.

examTips: Many failures on one account = brute force. Few failures on many accounts = spraying. This is the most common way the exam tests the difference.
Lockout stops brute force but does not stop spraying; MFA is the strongest answer for both.
Salting defeats rainbow tables; key stretching (bcrypt, PBKDF2, Argon2) slows offline cracking.
Offline attacks leave no failed-logon events; if the scenario involves stolen hashes, do not pick lockout as the fix.
videos.realWorld: Password spraying against Office 365, VPN and internet banking staff portals is a weekly event for Nigerian financial institutions, and SOC analysts rely on identity-provider sign-in logs and geo-velocity rules to catch it. After a successful spray, the analyst always checks for mailbox forwarding rules and new MFA devices because that is how attackers keep access. GRC teams set the password standard, push MFA coverage and legacy-authentication blocking as tracked control objectives, and confirm that application password storage uses salted, stretched hashing during vendor and internal application reviews.

quiz.q: Sign-in logs show a single external IP address attempting to log in to 800 different user accounts over six hours, with only one or two failed attempts per account and no lockouts triggered. Which attack is this?
options: Brute force against a single account
quiz.explain: A few common passwords tried across many accounts, deliberately staying below the lockout threshold, is password spraying. Brute force concentrates on one account, pass-the-hash uses stolen hashes rather than guesses, and rainbow tables are offline.

quiz.q: An attacker obtains a copy of a web application's user database containing unsalted MD5 password hashes. Which technique allows the attacker to recover most passwords fastest, and which storage practice would have prevented it?
options: Rainbow tables or GPU brute force; salted, key-stretched hashing such as bcrypt
quiz.explain: Unsalted fast hashes can be reversed with precomputed rainbow tables or brute-forced on GPUs at enormous speed. Per-user salts defeat precomputation and a slow hash like bcrypt makes each guess expensive. Lockout is irrelevant to an offline attack.

quiz.q: Windows Security logs show 3,000 Event ID 4625 failures for the account svc_backup from one internal workstation within ten minutes, followed by Event 4740. What has occurred?
options: A brute-force attack that triggered account lockout
quiz.explain: Thousands of failed logons for a single account from one source is online brute force, and Event 4740 confirms the account was locked out as a result. Spraying would touch many accounts, pass-the-hash would show successful NTLM logons, and birthday attacks concern hashes.

videos.title: Indicators of Compromise
videos.summary: Messer lists the observable signs that an attack may be underway: account lockouts, concurrent sessions, blocked content, impossible travel, resource consumption or inaccessibility, out-of-cycle logging, published data and missing logs.
videos.deepDive:
An indicator of compromise (IoC) is evidence that something malicious has happened or is happening. Some are atomic, such as a known-bad IP address or file hash. The ones on the SY0-701 list are behavioural: patterns in logs and systems that do not match how legitimate users and systems act. The exam gives you a scenario and expects you to name the indicator and, often, the attack behind it. Here is each one, with what it looks like and what it usually means.

Account lockout. One account locking repeatedly points to a brute-force attempt or a stale credential on a device. Many accounts locking at once points to a sprayer that misjudged the threshold or a deliberate denial-of-service against users. Look at Event 4740 and its caller computer name.

Concurrent session usage. The same account logged in from two places at once: a VPN session from Lagos while the user's badge shows them in the Abuja office, or two active web sessions from different countries. Legitimate causes exist (a phone and a laptop), so the analyst checks device, location and timing. It often indicates stolen credentials or a hijacked session token.

Blocked content. The proxy, firewall, EDR or mail gateway blocked something: a download from a malicious category, an outbound connection to a known command-and-control server, a quarantined attachment. A single block is routine. A pattern of blocks from one host, or blocks that follow a suspicious process launch, suggest malware already on the host trying to reach out. Blocked content is an early warning, not a resolution.

Impossible travel. A user authenticates from two locations separated by more distance than could be covered in the time between the logins. Identity providers compute this automatically. Common benign explanations are VPNs and cloud proxies, so the analyst confirms with the user or the device before treating it as account compromise.

Resource consumption. Unexplained spikes in CPU, memory, disk I/O, or network bandwidth. Cryptomining malware pins CPU. Ransomware causes heavy disk writes. Data exfiltration shows as a large, sustained outbound transfer, often at night, to a cloud storage service. Baseline the normal and alert on deviation.

Resource inaccessibility. Users cannot reach a service, files will not open, a server stops responding. Causes range from a DoS attack to ransomware encryption to an attacker deleting or disabling something. When several unrelated resources become inaccessible at once, treat it as an incident, not an outage.

Out-of-cycle logging. Activity at the wrong time: a scheduled job that normally runs at 02:00 running at 14:00, an administrator logging on at 03:00 on a Sunday, a backup job running twice. Attackers work when defenders are not watching, and they often trigger tasks manually.

Published or documented. Your data appears somewhere public: customer records on a leak site, credentials on a paste site, internal documents in a dark-web sale, or a threat actor announcing a breach. This is often the first an organisation learns of an intrusion. Threat intelligence and dark-web monitoring services exist to catch it early.

Missing logs. Gaps in a log, a cleared Security log (Event 1102 records the clearing), a host that stopped sending to the SIEM, or audit logging turned off. Attackers delete logs to cover tracks, so the absence of logs is itself evidence. Forward logs to a central, write-once store as they are generated so deletion on the host does not lose them.

Triage approach for any IoC: confirm the observation is real, establish the scope (which users, hosts, time window), find the earliest related event, decide whether it is benign, suspicious or malicious, and then contain. Individual indicators are weak; correlation is strong. Impossible travel plus a new mailbox forwarding rule plus blocked outbound content from the user's laptop is an incident, not three tickets.

keyTerms.def: Observable evidence such as an artefact or behaviour pattern that suggests a system or account has been attacked or breached.
Two authentications by one account from locations too far apart to be reached in the time between them.
One account active in multiple simultaneous sessions from different devices or locations, suggesting credential theft.
Log entries showing activity at times or frequencies outside the expected schedule for that system or user.
Gaps, cleared audit trails or silenced log sources, often the result of an attacker covering tracks.
Unexplained spikes in CPU, memory, disk or network use that may indicate cryptomining, ransomware or exfiltration.
Organisational data or credentials appearing on public, paste or dark-web sites, indicating a breach has already occurred.
A record of normal system and user behaviour against which anomalies can be detected.

examTips: Read for the exact indicator wording: two distant logins in a short time = impossible travel; one account in two places at once = concurrent session usage.
Missing or cleared logs are themselves an indicator; the control answer is centralised, tamper-resistant log forwarding.
Out-of-cycle logging is about timing, not content; a normal job at an abnormal time is the clue.
Published or documented means the data is already out; the response involves threat intelligence and breach notification, not prevention.
Blocked content shows a control worked but usually implies something upstream needs investigation.
videos.realWorld: These indicators are literally the alert names in a bank SOC's SIEM and identity platform: impossible travel, mass lockout, log source stopped reporting, unusual outbound volume. A tier-1 analyst's day is confirming or dismissing them with context, and the ones that survive become incidents. GRC analysts use the same list to design detection requirements, to check that log retention and integrity meet CBN and NDPA expectations, and to run breach-response procedures when customer data is found published, which triggers notification duties under the NDPA and reporting to the CBN.

quiz.q: A user's account authenticates to the VPN from Lagos at 09:00 and to the cloud email service from a European IP address at 09:25. The user is at her desk in Lagos. Which indicator does this represent?
quiz.explain: Two logins from locations that cannot be reached within the elapsed time is impossible travel and suggests the credentials are being used by someone else. The other indicators refer to timing patterns, system load and log gaps.

quiz.q: During an investigation, an analyst finds that the Windows Security event log on a file server contains no entries for a three-day period, and Event ID 1102 appears just after the gap. What should the analyst conclude?
options: The server was powered off for maintenance
The log was cleared, which is itself an indicator of compromise
quiz.explain: Event 1102 records that the audit log was cleared. A gap followed by a clear event indicates an attacker removing evidence. Power loss or disk exhaustion would not generate a clear event, and the log existing at all shows logging was enabled.

quiz.q: A database server that normally runs a nightly export at 01:00 shows the same export job executed at 15:30 on a weekday, followed by a large outbound transfer to an external cloud storage domain. Which two indicators are present?
options: Out-of-cycle logging and unusual resource consumption
quiz.explain: A scheduled job running outside its normal window is out-of-cycle logging, and the large unexpected outbound transfer is abnormal resource consumption consistent with data exfiltration. No lockouts, travel anomalies or log gaps are described.

objectives.title: Explain the purpose of mitigation techniques used to secure the enterprise

videos.title: Segmentation and Access Control
videos.summary: Messer explains how dividing a network into segments limits the spread of an attack, and how access control lists and permissions decide who and what can cross those boundaries.
videos.deepDive:
Segmentation and access control are the two mitigation techniques that decide how far an attacker can get after the first foothold. Every intrusion in the previous objective, from a macro virus on a teller's laptop to pass-the-hash lateral movement, depended on the compromised host being able to reach the next target. Segmentation reduces what is reachable; access control decides who may use what is reachable.

Segmentation means dividing a flat network into zones with enforced boundaries. Physical segmentation uses separate switches and cables, which is expensive but absolute; an air-gapped network for a SWIFT terminal or a card-key management system is the extreme case. Logical segmentation uses VLANs to separate traffic on shared switches, with a firewall or a layer-3 device controlling what passes between VLANs. Common zones in a bank: user workstations, servers, the card-data environment, management interfaces, guest Wi-Fi, and a screened subnet (DMZ) for internet-facing services. The purpose is twofold. It limits blast radius, so ransomware on the office LAN cannot reach the core banking database. And it makes monitoring easier, because traffic crossing a boundary can be inspected and unusual crossings stand out. PCI DSS explicitly rewards segmentation by shrinking the scope of systems that must meet its full requirements. Microsegmentation extends the idea down to the individual workload, using host firewalls or software-defined networking so that even two servers in the same subnet can talk only on approved ports.

Worked example: a fintech runs everything on one /22 subnet. A developer's laptop is compromised by a phishing attachment; the attacker scans the subnet, finds the production database listening on port 5432, and uses a password from a config file. After the incident, the company creates a production VLAN reachable only from a jump host that requires MFA, and a developer VLAN with no direct route to production. The same phishing attachment a year later gives the attacker a laptop and nothing else.

Access control lists (ACLs) are the rules on the boundaries. On a router or firewall an ACL says which source can reach which destination on which port: permit the application server to reach the database on 5432, deny everything else. Order matters, because most devices process rules top down and stop at the first match, and the implicit final rule is deny. On file systems, ACLs attach to files and folders and say which users or groups can read, write or execute. On cloud platforms, security groups and IAM policies play the same role. ACLs enforce the principle that access is denied unless explicitly allowed. Indicators of ACL trouble a SOC watches: deny-log entries showing a host repeatedly trying to cross a boundary it should not need to, and change-management logs for rules added outside a change window.

Permissions are the same concept at the object level: what a specific identity can do with a specific resource. Least privilege means giving only the permissions the role requires and nothing more. Permissions are commonly assigned through groups rather than to individuals so that joiners, movers and leavers are handled by group membership. Periodic access reviews confirm that permissions still match roles, which is one of the most audited controls in banking.

How they combine: segmentation decides which networks can talk, ACLs decide which traffic is allowed between them, and permissions decide what an authenticated user can do once connected. Defence in depth means all three, so that a failure in one is caught by the next. On the exam, when a scenario asks how to stop an attack spreading from one department to another, the answer is segmentation; when it asks how to limit which systems a server can talk to, the answer is an ACL; when it asks how to stop a user reading data they do not need, the answer is permissions with least privilege.

keyTerms.def: Dividing a network into separate zones, physically or with VLANs and firewalls, to contain attacks and control traffic flow.
A virtual LAN that logically separates traffic on shared switching hardware; inter-VLAN traffic must pass through a routing or firewall point.
A segment between the internet and the internal network that hosts public-facing services so they can be compromised without exposing internal systems.
Physical isolation of a system or network with no network connection to other networks.
Fine-grained segmentation down to individual workloads, often enforced by host firewalls or software-defined networking.
An ordered list of rules that permits or denies traffic or object access based on attributes such as source, destination, port or identity.
The default behaviour of an ACL to block anything not explicitly permitted.
Granting an identity only the permissions needed to perform its role and nothing more.

examTips: Stopping an attack from spreading between departments or from users to servers = segmentation.
Controlling which hosts and ports can communicate across a boundary = ACL; remember first-match processing and implicit deny.
Reducing PCI DSS scope is a classic reason given for segmenting the card-data environment.
Permissions questions usually have least privilege or group-based access as the correct answer.
videos.realWorld: In a Nigerian bank the card-processing environment, the core banking network and the general office LAN are separated by firewalls with tightly maintained ACLs, and the segmentation is tested annually because PCI DSS and CBN examiners ask for evidence. SOC analysts treat a workstation attempting to reach the server VLAN on ports it never uses as a high-priority alert, since it is one of the clearest signs of lateral movement. GRC analysts own the access review cycle, confirm firewall rule changes go through change management, and keep the network zoning diagram current for audits.

quiz.q: After a ransomware incident spread from the marketing department to the finance file servers, management asks for a control that would prevent a compromised workstation in one department from reaching servers in another. Which is the best answer?
options: Network segmentation with firewall rules between zones
quiz.explain: Segmentation with controlled boundaries stops traffic from one zone reaching another unless explicitly allowed, containing the spread. Passwords, encryption at rest and training do not restrict network reachability.

quiz.q: A firewall ACL contains a rule at the top permitting all traffic from the user VLAN to the server VLAN, followed by a rule denying the user VLAN access to the database server. Users can still reach the database. Why?
options: Implicit deny overrides the explicit deny
The deny rule is missing a port
ACLs are processed top down and the first matching permit rule applies
The database server is on the wrong VLAN
quiz.explain: Most firewalls stop at the first matching rule. The broad permit at the top matches before the specific deny is ever evaluated, so the deny rule must be moved above it. The other options do not explain the behaviour.

quiz.q: A junior accountant can open the HR salary spreadsheet on a shared drive even though her role does not require it. Which mitigation technique is not being applied correctly?
quiz.explain: The user holds a permission her role does not need, which violates least privilege. Segmentation controls network reachability, not file access, and patching and encryption are unrelated to who is authorised to read the file.

videos.title: Mitigation Techniques
videos.summary: Messer surveys the enterprise mitigation toolkit: application allow lists, isolation, patching, encryption, monitoring, least privilege, configuration enforcement and decommissioning.
videos.deepDive:
This video lists the general-purpose mitigations the exam expects you to match to a scenario. Each one addresses a specific weakness that the attacks in objective 2.4 exploit. The skill being tested is choosing the most direct mitigation, not just any control that helps.

Application allow list. Only approved executables and scripts may run; everything else is blocked by default. This is the opposite of a block list, which tries to enumerate what is bad and always misses something new. Allow listing is the single most effective control against malicious code and unknown malware, which is why it is standard on servers, ATMs and point-of-sale devices. The cost is administration: every new legitimate program needs approval, so it is easier to deploy on servers with a stable software set than on developer laptops.

Isolation. Cutting a system off from others so it can neither be attacked nor attack. It can be permanent, such as an air-gapped key-management server, or temporary, such as an EDR agent quarantining a compromised laptop so it can only reach the SOC's investigation tools. Sandboxes isolate untrusted code while it is examined. On the exam, if a host is confirmed compromised and the question asks for the immediate action, isolation is usually right.

Patching. Applying vendor fixes removes the vulnerabilities that worms, exploits and privilege escalation rely on. A patch management process includes inventory, prioritisation by severity and exposure, testing, deployment and verification. The gap between patch release and installation is the attacker's window; WannaCry and the Equifax breach both exploited vulnerabilities with patches available for months. Internet-facing and privileged systems get patched first.

Encryption. Data at rest (full-disk, database, file-level) protects against theft of the storage medium and reduces breach impact. Data in transit (TLS, VPN, SSH) defeats on-path interception. Encryption does not stop an attacker who has valid credentials, so it is a confidentiality control, not an access control.

Monitoring. Collecting logs, metrics and alerts into a SIEM so that indicators of compromise are seen and acted on. Prevention will fail eventually; monitoring is what turns a silent breach into a managed incident. It requires deciding what to log, forwarding it centrally, protecting it from tampering, and having people and rules to look at it.

Least privilege. Every user, process and service account gets only the rights required. It limits what malware can do when it runs under a user's account, reduces the value of a stolen credential, and shrinks the damage an insider can cause. Removing local administrator rights from workstations is the highest-impact single step.

Configuration enforcement. Defining a secure baseline, applying it automatically through group policy, mobile device management or configuration management tools, and detecting and reverting drift. A baseline that is documented but not enforced decays within weeks as people make local changes. Compliance scanning against the baseline produces the evidence auditors want.

Decommissioning. Properly retiring systems, applications and accounts that are no longer needed. Forgotten servers stop being patched, orphaned accounts keep their passwords forever, and old domains get re-registered by attackers. Decommissioning includes removing from the network, revoking credentials and certificates, sanitising or destroying storage media, and updating the asset inventory.

Worked example: a Nigerian microfinance bank suffers an intrusion through a former staff member's VPN account that was never disabled (decommissioning failure). The attacker runs a credential-dumping tool on a server (an allow list would have blocked it), escalates using a vulnerability patched eight months earlier (patching failure), and reads customer records from an unencrypted export folder (encryption failure). No alert fired because the server was not sending logs (monitoring failure). Each failure maps to one technique on this list; the exam scenario will usually describe one of them and ask you to name the missing control.

keyTerms.def: A control permitting only explicitly approved software to execute, blocking all other programs and scripts by default.
Separating a system from the network or other systems, permanently or temporarily, so it cannot be reached or reach others.
The process of identifying, prioritising, testing, deploying and verifying vendor fixes for vulnerabilities.
Automatically applying a secure baseline and correcting drift so systems stay in the approved state.
Formally retiring a system or account by removing network access, revoking credentials and sanitising storage.
Continuous collection and analysis of logs and metrics to detect and respond to indicators of compromise.
An isolated environment where untrusted code or files can be executed and observed without affecting production systems.
The gradual divergence of a system from its approved baseline through unmanaged changes.

examTips: Unknown or novel malware ran on a server = application allow list is the strongest preventive answer.
Compromised host, immediate action required = isolation.
The attack exploited a known vulnerability = patching; a stolen laptop or database = encryption at rest.
Old accounts or forgotten servers used in an attack = decommissioning failure.
Systems drifting from the secure baseline = configuration enforcement, not a one-time hardening.
videos.realWorld: A SOC lives inside the monitoring and isolation techniques: analysts quarantine hosts via EDR, block indicators, and escalate. GRC owns the rest as control objectives with evidence: patch SLA reports, allow-list coverage on in-scope servers, encryption inventories, baseline compliance scans, and a decommissioning checklist signed off for every retired system. CBN risk-based examinations and PCI DSS assessments at Nigerian banks routinely sample all of these, and the most common findings are unpatched internet-facing systems and orphaned accounts.

quiz.q: A server was compromised by a new strain of malware that no antivirus vendor had a signature for. Which control would most directly have prevented the malware from executing?
quiz.explain: Allow listing blocks any executable that has not been explicitly approved, regardless of whether it is recognised as malicious. Encryption, segmentation and passwords do not control which programs run on the host.

quiz.q: A former contractor's VPN account was used six months after his contract ended to access internal systems. Which mitigation technique was neglected?
quiz.explain: Accounts and access belonging to people who have left must be revoked as part of decommissioning. Patching, encryption and isolation do not address dormant credentials.

quiz.q: An audit finds that 30 percent of workstations no longer match the approved security baseline because users and technicians have changed settings over time. Which technique addresses this problem on an ongoing basis?
quiz.explain: Configuration enforcement continuously applies the baseline and corrects drift, whereas a one-off hardening effort would decay again. The other techniques do not maintain settings over time.

videos.title: Hardening Techniques
videos.summary: Messer explains how to reduce a system's attack surface: encryption, endpoint protection, host-based firewalls and intrusion prevention, disabling unnecessary ports and protocols, changing default passwords and removing unnecessary software.
videos.deepDive:
Hardening is the process of configuring a single system so that it exposes as little as possible to attack. A freshly installed operating system or appliance is built for convenience: services are on, default accounts exist, and everything is reachable. Hardening reverses that. The techniques on the objective are the standard checklist; a real hardening standard such as the CIS Benchmarks contains hundreds of settings, but every one of them fits into one of these categories.

Encryption. Full-disk encryption (BitLocker, FileVault, LUKS) protects data if the device is lost or the drive is removed; a stolen laptop with an encrypted disk is a hardware loss, not a data breach. File and database encryption protect specific sensitive data. Encryption is only as good as key management: a BitLocker key stored on a sticky note or a database key in the same directory as the database defeats the purpose.

Endpoint protection. Antivirus, anti-malware and modern EDR on every host. EDR watches process behaviour, network connections and memory, reports to a central console, and can isolate the host. Coverage matters: the one server without an agent is where the attacker will be found.

Host-based firewall. A firewall on the system itself, filtering inbound and outbound connections regardless of where the device is. It enforces microsegmentation and protects a laptop on hotel Wi-Fi as well as a server in the data centre. The rule set should permit only the services the host actually provides; a database server has no reason to accept inbound connections on anything but its database port from anything but its application servers.

Host-based intrusion prevention system (HIPS). Software that inspects activity on the host, such as system calls, file changes and network traffic, against rules or behaviour models and blocks what looks malicious. It is the difference between logging an exploit attempt (HIDS) and stopping it (HIPS). Modern EDR platforms include HIPS functions such as exploit protection and ransomware rollback.

Disabling ports and protocols. Every listening service is an entry point. Run netstat -an or ss -tlnp, compare against what the system is for, and disable the rest: Telnet, FTP, SMBv1, NetBIOS, unused web management interfaces, SNMP with default community strings. The same applies to legacy protocols on the network: block LLMNR and NBT-NS, which attackers abuse to capture hashes. Fewer open ports means fewer vulnerabilities to patch and fewer things to monitor.

Default password changes. Routers, switches, cameras, printers, IoT devices and many applications ship with documented default credentials. The Mirai botnet built itself almost entirely from devices still using them. Change every default on installation, and disable or rename default administrative accounts where possible. A vulnerability scanner will flag defaults it can detect, but a manual check during commissioning is the reliable control.

Removal of unnecessary software. Every installed package is code that can have vulnerabilities and must be patched. Remove bloatware, sample applications, compilers on production servers, and any feature not required for the system's role. Windows Server Core and minimal Linux images exist precisely to start from a smaller footprint.

Worked example: a Nigerian fintech commissions a new payment API server. The hardening checklist applied before it goes live: disk encrypted; EDR agent installed and reporting; host firewall allowing inbound only 443 from the load balancer and 22 from the jump host; SSH root login disabled and password authentication replaced with keys; Telnet, FTP and unused services removed; default database and application admin passwords changed and stored in the vault; sample web content and unused packages removed; the result scanned against the CIS benchmark and the report attached to the change ticket. Six months later a vulnerability scan shows the host drifting from the baseline, which is where configuration enforcement from the previous video takes over.

How this is tested: the exam gives a scenario with a specific weakness and asks for the hardening technique that fixes it. A device compromised with factory credentials = change default passwords. An attacker used Telnet = disable unnecessary protocols. A lost laptop = full-disk encryption. Malware ran on a host without being stopped = endpoint protection or HIPS. A server accepted connections from any host = host-based firewall.

keyTerms.def: Configuring a system to minimise its attack surface by removing, disabling or securing everything not required for its role.
Encrypting an entire storage device so data is unreadable without the key, protecting against physical theft.
Endpoint software that continuously monitors behaviour, detects threats, and enables remote investigation and isolation.
A firewall running on an individual system that filters its own inbound and outbound connections.
Software on a host that detects and actively blocks malicious activity such as exploit attempts or unauthorised changes.
Factory-set usernames and passwords that are publicly documented and must be changed on installation.
Consensus-based, published secure configuration guides for operating systems, applications and devices used as hardening standards.
Removing services, software, ports and accounts so there are fewer ways for an attacker to reach a system.

examTips: Device compromised using factory or documented credentials = change default passwords.
Attack came in over Telnet, FTP, SMBv1 or an unused management port = disable unnecessary ports and protocols.
HIDS detects and alerts; HIPS detects and blocks. If the question wants prevention on the host, pick HIPS.
Lost or stolen device with sensitive data = full-disk encryption is the hardening answer.
Removing unnecessary software is the hardening fix for bloatware and for vulnerabilities in packages the system never needed.
videos.realWorld: Hardening standards are among the first documents a GRC analyst at a bank maintains, usually derived from CIS Benchmarks and mapped to CBN, PCI DSS and ISO 27001 requirements, with compliance scans as the evidence. SOC analysts feel the results directly: a well-hardened estate produces fewer alerts and clearer ones, because there is no legacy protocol noise and no unexplained listening service. Default credentials on network devices and cameras remain one of the most common findings in Nigerian internal penetration tests, which is why commissioning checklists exist.

quiz.q: A penetration tester gains administrative access to several branch office routers using the username admin and the password admin. Which hardening technique would have prevented this?
quiz.explain: The devices were still using factory credentials. Changing defaults at installation is the direct fix. Firewalls, disk encryption and software removal do not address known default logins.

quiz.q: A vulnerability scan of a database server shows Telnet, FTP and an unused web administration interface all listening, in addition to the database port. Which action best reduces the server's attack surface?
options: Disable the unnecessary ports and protocols
quiz.explain: Each listening service is a potential entry point. Disabling those not required for the server's role removes vulnerabilities and reduces what must be monitored. The other options do not close the exposed services.

quiz.q: An organisation wants software on each server that will not only detect an exploit attempt against a running process but actively block it in real time. Which control meets this requirement?
quiz.explain: A HIPS detects and blocks malicious activity on the host, whereas a HIDS only detects and alerts. Disk encryption protects data at rest and network access control governs which devices may join the network.
